### How payments work on SDP
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/concepts

> The wallets, tokens, signing, fees, and records behind an SDP payment.

An SDP payment moves value between two Solana accounts. A custody wallet sends tokens to a
destination address, and SDP records the transfer.

This page explains the parts that the rest of this section assumes: wallets, tokens, execution,
fees, and the transfer record.

## Custody wallets

Every SDP payment starts from a **custody wallet**. A custody wallet is a Solana wallet that SDP
manages for an organization, and optionally for one project inside it.

A custody provider holds the key and signs with it. SDP gives you one stable Solana address and
sends each signing request to the provider that holds the key. The wallet signs your outbound
transfers. It also reports balances and applies policies for the addresses you control.

Create your custody wallets before you send a payment. See
[Set up wallets](/docs/guides/setup-wallets).

A transfer request passes the SDP wallet `id` (`cwlt_…`) as `sourceCustodyWalletId`. The response
returns the same value as `custodyWalletId`, and keeps the provider's own identifier separately as
`providerWalletId`. The `destination` is always the recipient's Solana address.

Ramp quote endpoints use the same fields for every provider. An onramp quote takes
`destinationCustodyWalletId`. An offramp quote takes `sourceCustodyWalletId`. Both identify a
custody wallet you control, by the `id` that `GET /v1/wallets` returns.

SDP resolves provider-specific identifiers, such as a customer ID or a payout account ID, from the
counterparty's provider requirements. See [Ramps](/docs/payments/ramps).

## Tokens and token accounts

A payment transfers **SPL tokens**. These can be stablecoins, tokenized assets, or any other mint
your project supports.

On `POST /v1/payments/transfers`, the `token` field takes the **mint address**. For native SOL,
pass the string `SOL`. SDP does not resolve a symbol such as `USDC` when it receives the request.

On `GET /v1/payments/transfers`, the `token` filter matches the stored `Transfer.token` value
exactly. A transfer created through the API stores the mint you supplied, or `SOL`. A transfer that
SDP observed onchain can store a resolved symbol instead, such as `USDC`.

Filter with the same label that the response shows. You can also omit `token` and filter the
results in your own code.

Balance responses behave differently. They always try to resolve the symbol, and return it whenever
SDP knows the mint. A wallet that holds USDC therefore reports `USDC`, not the mint address.

**Every amount in a request is a decimal string in display units.** `"100.00"` means 100 tokens,
whatever the mint's decimal count is. This rule covers payment transfers and issuance operations
such as mint, burn, seize, and force-burn. SDP converts the value to the smallest unit when it
builds the transaction.

Wallet balance responses are the one exception. They return a raw `amount` in the smallest unit and
a `uiAmount` as a decimal string, so you can use whichever one you need.

## Transfer execution

SDP executes an outbound wallet transfer when you call `POST /v1/payments/transfers`. SDP builds
the transaction, signs it with the source wallet's custody key, and submits it to the configured
Solana cluster. SDP then records the transfer and tracks its status.

The rest of this section assumes that SDP submits the transfer from a custody wallet you control.

## Fees and sponsorship

The fee payer of a transaction pays the Solana fee in SOL. On a wallet transfer, the source custody
wallet is the fee payer by default.

You can configure SDP to sponsor the fee instead. An end-user wallet then does not need a SOL
balance.

## The transfer data model

Every transfer creates a `Transfer` record, whether it succeeds or fails. These are the fields that
matter in most flows.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | SDP-internal transfer identifier (use this in API URLs). |
| `status` | Wallet transfers: `processing`, `confirmed`, `finalized`, `failed`. Ramp transfers: `pending`, `awaiting_payment`, `settling`, `completed`, `canceled`, `expired`, `failed`. See [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification). |
| `direction` | `inbound` (someone paid you) or `outbound` (you paid someone). |
| `source`, `destination` | Solana addresses. |
| `token`, `amount` | What moved, and how much. `amount` is a decimal string in display units, for example `"100.00"`. |
| `memo` | Optional UTF-8 string, up to 256 chars. See [Payment with memo](/docs/payments/send-payment-with-memo). |
| `signature` | The Solana transaction signature, set once the transfer is confirmed. It is unique across SDP, so use it as the deduplication key. |
| `slot`, `blockTime`, `fee` | Settlement details from the network, filled in as the transaction lands. |
| `error` | Set when the transfer fails. The rest of the record shows what reached the network. |
| `risk` | Risk score metadata. Present only when a risk provider is configured. |

An outbound wallet transfer starts at `processing`, then moves to `confirmed` and then
`finalized`. An inbound transfer that SDP finds onchain appears at `confirmed`. A ramp transfer can
start at `pending` while the provider completes its own steps.

See [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification#status-lifecycle) for the full state
table.

## What SDP does and does not give you

SDP gives you what you need to send, track, and reconcile payments at the level of a single
transfer:

- Status polling.
- Filtered transfer lists.
- Balances per wallet.
- Replay of a request through the `Idempotency-Key` header, per wallet.
- A unique `signature` once the network confirms the transaction. See
  [Basic payment](/docs/payments/send-basic-payment#deduplication).

SDP does not give you commerce objects such as a checkout session or an invoice. The
[Accept payments](/docs/payments/accept-overview) section shows how to build those on top of the
transfer record.

## Related

- [Payments API reference](/docs/reference/api/payments). The generated endpoint reference.
- [End-to-end payment flow](/docs/tutorials/end-to-end-payment-flow). The same lifecycle as a
  step-by-step tutorial.

## Payments — Send payments

### Basic payment
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/send-basic-payment

> Send a single token transfer from a custody wallet to a Solana address.

SDP handles token transfers through its Payments API. A basic payment moves tokens from a custody
wallet you control to any Solana wallet address.

`sourceCustodyWalletId` is the SDP wallet `id` (`cwlt_…`). `GET /v1/wallets` returns it. SDP
resolves it on the server from the caller's list of custody wallets.

`destination` is the recipient's Solana wallet address, also called the owner address. For SPL
token transfers, SDP derives the associated token account from this address. SDP creates that
account if it does not exist.

Pass the wallet address. Do not pass a token account address.

You can send a transfer from the dashboard or from the API.

## Prerequisites

- A deployed token with minted supply.
- A custody wallet to use as `sourceCustodyWalletId`. It needs a custody signer configured, so that
  SDP can sign and submit the transaction.
- An API key with both the `payments:write` and `wallets:read` permissions. The route layer for
  `POST /v1/payments/transfers` checks for that pair. SDP then re-checks the source wallet against
  the wallet scope of the key's `payments:write` permission, so that scope must include the source
  wallet.

## How it works

<HowItWorks>

<Step number={1} title="Set up the transfer">

Specify the source, the destination, the token, and the amount.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

Go to **Payments** in the sidebar. The overview shows your total SDP balance, your recent
transactions, and the **Send** and **Receive** actions.

![Payments overview showing the total balance, the Send and Receive actions, and the recent transactions list](/images/tokens/transfer-confirmed.png)

Select **Send**, then select **Onchain transfer** to send from an SDP wallet to a Solana address.

![Send page showing the Onchain transfer and Pay with fiat options](/images/tokens/transfer-send-options.png)

On the **What would you like to send?** step, select a source wallet from the dropdown.

![Transfer details step with the source wallet dropdown open](/images/tokens/transfer-form-source.png)

Enter the following values:

- **Source wallet.** A wallet you control in SDP.
- **Amount.** Display units, for example `0.5`.
- **Asset.** One of your deployed tokens.
- **Destination.** Any valid Solana wallet address.
- **Memo (optional).** A note that SDP records with the transfer.

![Transfer details step with every field filled in](/images/tokens/transfer-form-filled.png)

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

Build the request body:

```typescript title="transfer-request.ts"
const body = {
  sourceCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_123",    // `id` from GET /v1/wallets
  destination: "7xKXz...9fGh",         // recipient wallet (owner) address
  token: "9aBCd...4eEf",               // onchain mint address
  amount: "100.00",                    // human-readable units
  memo: "Payment for invoice #1234",
};
```

`token` is the mint address that the deploy step returned. It is not the SDP token ID.
`destination` is the wallet address, and SDP derives the associated token account from it.


```typescript title="execute-transfer.ts"
    method: "POST",

      "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",

      destination: "7xKXz...9fGh",
      token: "9aBCd...4eEf",
      amount: "100.00",
```

## Deduplication

Send one stable `Idempotency-Key` for each logical payment, and reuse that key for network
retries.

An identical request for the same exact `sourceCustodyWalletId` returns the original transfer. If
you reuse the key with a different payload, or with a different wallet, the API returns `409`. A
request with no key creates a new transfer intent.

Persist the returned `Transfer.id` as your local primary key. Once SDP sets the onchain
`signature`, that value is also unique across SDP transfers. You can use it to deduplicate records
across SDP and another chain indexer.

See [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts#dedup-and-retries) for the same pattern
applied to batched outbound flows.

### Payment with memo
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/send-payment-with-memo

> Attach an order ID, an invoice number, or a customer reference to an SDP transfer.

The `memo` field on `POST /v1/payments/transfers` carries a UTF-8 string of your choice alongside
the onchain transfer. A memo can be up to 256 characters.

SDP stores the memo on the `Transfer` record, and returns it in list and read responses. Your
indexer can therefore map each transfer back to a row in your own product database.

## When to use a memo

Use a memo when you need a free-form correlation value that your backend already knows at request
time:

- **Order IDs and invoice IDs.** A value such as `order_2026-05-14_4837` ties the transfer to a
  checkout row.
- **Customer references.** Your internal customer or account identifiers, for support and
  reconciliation.
- **Run identifiers.** A payout-batch ID shared across many outbound transfers in one
  disbursement.

SDP stores the memo on its own record. SDP does not attach it as a Solana memo-program
instruction. If you need an onchain memo that a block explorer displays, handle that at the
transaction level. See the trade-offs section below.

## API usage

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
    "destination": "7xKXz...9fGh",
    "token": "9aBCd...4eEf",
    "amount": "100.00",
    "memo": "order_2026-05-14_4837"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="send-payment-with-memo.ts"
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      sourceCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_123",
      destination: "7xKXz...9fGh",
      token: "9aBCd...4eEf",
      amount: "100.00",
      memo: "order_2026-05-14_4837",
    }),
  }
);
const { data } = await response.json();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="SendPaymentWithMemo.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        {
          "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
          "destination": "7xKXz...9fGh",
          "token": "9aBCd...4eEf",
          "amount": "100.00",
          "memo": "order_2026-05-14_4837"
        }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

SDP keeps the memo on the transfer record:

```json title="response.json"
{
  "id": "xfr_...",
  "memo": "order_2026-05-14_4837",
  "status": "finalized",
  "signature": "5xR1...",
  ...
}
```

A memo can be up to 256 characters. SDP accepts UTF-8. Trim or sanitize the value before you send
it if your downstream systems are stricter.

## Trade-offs against Solana Pay reference accounts

For accept flows, a **Solana Pay reference account** is an alternative way to correlate. You
generate a unique pubkey for each order and include it in the onchain transfer as a reference.

This has two advantages. The link has onchain provenance, so anyone can verify it without trusting
the SDP database. The payer can also build the transfer themselves from a Solana Pay URL.

SDP does not attach a Solana Pay reference onchain today, and SDP does not return one on an
inbound transfer record. Use `memo` for correlation inside SDP, or read the reference from the
transaction through Solana RPC. See [Accept payments](/docs/payments/accept-overview) and
[Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) for the inbound side.

As a rule: a memo is simpler when you initiate the transfer, as in a server-side payout or an
internal move. A reference is stronger when a third party initiates the transfer, as in a customer
checkout or a donation.

## Indexing implications

`GET /v1/payments/transfers` and `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{id}` both return the memo. Your
reconciliation worker can filter by date, direction, or token, and then match each row to your
order table by memo. See [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) for the
query patterns.

## Related

- [Basic payment](/docs/payments/send-basic-payment). The underlying transfer endpoint.
- [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts). Use a memo to tag a batch.
- [Accept payments](/docs/payments/accept-overview). When to use a reference account instead.

### Payouts and disbursements
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/send-payouts

> Run batched outbound transfers, deduplicate retries, and reconcile a payout batch with SDP.

A payout run is a batch of outbound transfers. Marketplace seller payouts, payroll, affiliate
disbursements, and royalty distributions are all payout runs.

Use `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches` when every recipient is a registered counterparty
account. For arbitrary Solana addresses, call `POST /v1/payments/transfers` once per recipient, and
reconcile the transfer IDs that it returns.

## Native transfer batches

One request creates a durable batch. SDP splits the recipients into Solana transactions, and
returns the batch record, the recipient records, and the transfer records.

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfer-batches \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: payroll-2026-05-14" \
  -d '{
    "externalId": "payroll_2026-05-14",
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
    "token": "9aBCd...4eEf",
    "recipients": [
      {
        "externalId": "row_4837",
        "counterpartyId": "cp_4837",
        "counterpartyAccountId": "cpa_4837",
        "amount": "150.00"
      }
    ]
  }'
```

Reuse the same `Idempotency-Key` when you retry that exact request. Call
`GET /v1/payments/transfer-batches/{batchId}` to inspect the recipient outcomes and the chunk
outcomes. `externalId` is a correlation field. It is not an idempotency key.

The rest of this page covers the per-recipient alternative, for destinations that are not
registered counterparty accounts.

## Designing a payout run

A typical run works like this.

1. **Resolve the recipients** in your application. List or stream the rows to be paid. Each row
   carries a destination address and an amount.
2. **Pick a batch identifier** that you control, such as
   `payout_2026-05-14_marketplace_sellers`.
3. **Iterate.** For each recipient, call `POST /v1/payments/transfers` with the destination, the
   amount, the token, and a memo. Encode the batch ID and a per-row identifier in the memo, as in
   `payout_2026-05-14_marketplace_sellers/row_4837`.
4. **Capture** the returned `Transfer.id` and `Transfer.status`. Persist the SDP transfer ID next
   to the recipient row, so that you can poll the status again later.
5. **Reconcile.** Once you have submitted the whole batch, call
   `GET /v1/payments/transfers?direction=outbound&from=…&to=…`. Confirm that every row in your
   application has a matching `finalized` transfer.

Send the transfers one at a time, or with modest concurrency of 4 to 8 in flight. High concurrency
raises the chance of priority-fee contention and blockhash expiry, and it adds little throughput.

## Dedup and retries

Two layers protect you against a double spend if a worker dies part-way through a run.

1. **Idempotency keys.** Generate one stable `Idempotency-Key` for each recipient row, and reuse
   it for retries. An identical request for the same exact source wallet returns the original
   transfer. If you reuse the key for a different request, the API returns `409`.
2. **Application mapping.** Persist the SDP transfer ID for each recipient row before you move to
   the next row. On restart, replay the row with the same idempotency key, or skip any row that
   already has a `Transfer.id`.

The onchain `signature` is unique across SDP transfers once SDP sets it. Use it as a
cross-indexer integrity check, not as the retry mechanism.

A fresh idempotency key creates a new transfer intent, even when the payload is otherwise
identical.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: payout-row-4837" \
  -d '{
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
    "destination": "7xKXz...9fGh",
    "token": "9aBCd...4eEf",
    "amount": "150.00",
    "memo": "payout_2026-05-14_marketplace_sellers/row_4837"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="payout-recipient.ts"
async function payoutRecipient(row: PayoutRow): Promise<string> {
  if (row.transferId) return row.transferId; // already submitted

  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers",
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": row.idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        sourceCustodyWalletId: row.sourceCustodyWalletId,
        destination: row.destination,
        token: row.token,
        amount: row.amount,
        memo: `${row.batchId}/row_${row.id}`,
      }),
    }
  );

  const { data } = await response.json();
  // The transfer record is under data.transfer (standard SDP success envelope).
  await row.persistTransferId(data.transfer.id); // persist BEFORE returning
  return data.transfer.id;
}
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="PayoutRecipient.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .header("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        {
          "sourceCustodyWalletId": "%s",
          "destination": "%s",
          "token": "%s",
          "amount": "%s",
          "memo": "%s/row_%s"
        }""".formatted(sourceCustodyWalletId, destination, token, amount, batchId, rowId)))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Reconciling a run

After the loop finishes, list every outbound transfer in the time window of the run. Then tally
the list against your recipient table.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers?direction=outbound&from=2026-05-14T00:00:00Z&to=2026-05-14T23:59:59Z&pageSize=100" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="list-outbound-transfers.ts"
async function* listOutboundTransfers(from: string, to: string) {
  let page = 1;
  while (true) {
    const url = new URL("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers");
    url.searchParams.set("direction", "outbound");
    url.searchParams.set("from", from);
    url.searchParams.set("to", to);
    url.searchParams.set("page", String(page));
    url.searchParams.set("pageSize", "100");

    const res = await fetch(url, {
      headers: { Authorization: "Bearer sk_test_..." },
    });
    const { data, meta } = await res.json();
    yield* data;
    if (!meta.hasMore) return;
    page += 1;
  }
}
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Scope the result to the batch by filtering on `memo.startsWith(batchId)`, or on whatever
convention you chose. Then cross-reference each recipient row by its SDP `Transfer.id`.

## Failure modes

Expect to handle these per-transfer outcomes.

- **`failed`.** SDP built and submitted the transaction, and the network rejected it. Common
  causes are insufficient funds, a frozen account, and an expired blockhash. The `error` field on
  the transfer record explains what reached the chain. The recipient was not paid. You can retry
  by submitting a new transfer.
- **`pending` past the expected confirmation window.** This is usually a backend or RPC problem.
  Poll `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{id}` again rather than submitting again. Create a new transfer
  only if the status settles to `failed`.
- **A worker crash part-way through the run.** Resume with each row's original `Idempotency-Key`.
  Persist the returned `Transfer.id` before you advance to the next row.
- **The source wallet runs out of SOL for fees.** Submissions start to fail with fee-related
  errors. This does not happen when SDP is configured to sponsor fees. Otherwise, top up the SOL
  balance of the source wallet before you continue.

- [Basic payment](/docs/payments/send-basic-payment). The underlying transfer endpoint.
- [Payment with memo](/docs/payments/send-payment-with-memo). The memo field used above to tag a
  batch.

  inbound.
- [Wallet policies](/docs/wallet-operations/policies). Destination allowlists and daily limits for
  a payout wallet.

## Payments — Accept payments

### Accept payments
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/accept-overview

> Publish a receiving address, detect the inbound transfer, and match it to an order.

SDP does not provide a hosted checkout product. To accept a payment, you publish a Solana address
that you control. SDP detects the inbound transfer and returns it in the transfer list.

This page covers that pattern. [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification) and
[Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) cover the details.

## Receiving-address convention

The receiving address is a custody wallet you control. Choose one of two scopes.

**One wallet per order.** This is the recommended scope for accept flows. Create a fresh custody
wallet, or a sub-account, for each order or for each customer. The destination address is then your
correlation key. The `destination` field on the inbound transfer maps one-to-one to your order row,
so you do not depend on a memo field or a reference field.

**One wallet per merchant scope.** For a marketplace, create one custody wallet per seller. For
treasury operations, create one per ledger account. This scope is reasonable when you do not need
correlation, as in treasury and settlement work, or when each merchant takes a single fixed-amount
payment.

The address you publish is the onchain `address` of the custody wallet. Fetch it with
[`GET /v1/wallets/{walletId}`](/docs/reference/api/wallets). Add `?includeBalance=false` when you
need only the wallet metadata. That skips a balance RPC call and a pricing lookup.

Senders use that address as the destination of a normal SPL token transfer. SDP indexes the inbound
transfer and returns it from [`GET /v1/payments/transfers`](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) with
`direction=inbound`.

**Correlation caveats.** SDP does not populate `Transfer.memo` for a customer-initiated inbound
transfer. SDP does not extract Solana memo-program instructions into the record, and the inbound
record carries no reference field either.

The `memo` field is optional in the schema rather than nullable. SDP therefore omits it from the
response instead of returning `null`. SDP populates `memo` only for a transfer that SDP itself
initiated, whether outbound or internal.

The reliable correlation key on the record is the inbound transfer's `destination`. That is the
reason for the per-order receiving address above. If you need correlation by memo or by reference,
for example for a Solana Pay URL that carries an order pubkey, read the onchain transaction through
Solana RPC using the transfer's `signature`.

## Integration options

A customer can land a payment on the address you control in two ways.

1. **Direct address share.** You display the address, the expected token, and the expected amount
   in your own screens. The customer's wallet sends the transfer. This works with any Solana wallet
   and any client, because SDP picks the transfer up from the chain. Use it for B2B settlement,
   treasury operations, and crypto-native flows.
2. **Solana Pay request.** For consumer checkout, give the customer a
   [Solana Pay](https://solana.com/docs/payments/accept-payments/solana-pay) URL or QR code. It
   carries the destination, the amount, and a per-order `reference` pubkey. The customer's wallet
   builds the transfer and attaches the `reference` account onchain. You then match the transfer
   back to the order by reading the transaction through Solana RPC, because neither the `reference`
   nor a wallet-set memo reaches the SDP `Transfer` record. See the
   [correlation caveats](#receiving-address-convention) above. SDP does not host a Solana Pay
   endpoint today, and SDP does not attach a Solana Pay reference onchain. See
   [Solana Pay reference accounts](/docs/payments/accept-indexing#solana-pay-reference-accounts-roadmap).
   For correlation inside SDP today, use a per-order destination address.

## What SDP gives you today

- **Indexed inbound transfers.** `GET /v1/payments/transfers?direction=inbound` returns the
  persisted transfers across your custody wallets. Filter by exact `custodyWalletId`. Add
  `includeObserved=true` to include recent chain observations for that wallet. See
  [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing).
- **Per-transfer status reads.** `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{id}` returns the lifecycle of one
  payment. See [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification).
- **Wallet balances.** `GET /v1/payments/wallets/{walletId}/balances` returns the current per-token
  balance on a receiving wallet. See [Wallet balances](/docs/wallet-operations/balances).
- **Address-based correlation.** The `destination` on the inbound transfer is the correlation key
  held on the record. Pair it with a per-order receiving address to map an inbound transfer to an
  order without a memo. See the [correlation caveats](#receiving-address-convention) above.

## What SDP does not give you yet

- **No checkout session and no payment intent object.** You do not pre-register an expected payment
  with the API. SDP recognizes an inbound transfer after the fact, and you match it on the
  `destination` held on the record. The token and the amount are available as extra checks. See the
  [correlation caveats](#receiving-address-convention) above.
- **No webhooks on settlement.** Observe a status change by polling
  `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{id}`, or by listing again with date filters. See the
  [polling cadence guidance](/docs/payments/accept-verification#polling-cadence).
- **No hosted Solana Pay URL endpoint.** To serve a Solana Pay URL or QR code, build it in your own
  client from the destination address, the token mint, the amount, and the reference pubkey.

## Worked example: a marketplace checkout

This is the smallest accept flow built on the per-order-address pattern.

1. At checkout, create a fresh custody wallet for the order, or claim one from a warm pool.
2. Stage a row in your `orders` table. Store that wallet's onchain address, the expected amount,
   and the token.
3. Show the customer the per-order custody wallet address, the token, and the amount. Build a
   Solana Pay URL from those fields if you want a QR code. No SDP endpoint is involved.
4. The customer's wallet submits the transfer.
5. Your reconciliation worker lists recent persisted inbound transfers on a schedule. To discover
   chain activity that SDP has not persisted yet, poll each receiving wallet with its exact
   `custodyWalletId` and `includeObserved=true`. Match each transfer's `destination` to an open
   order in your `orders` table.
6. When a transfer matches, mark the order paid and ship the goods. Use the transfer's `signature`
   to deduplicate if the worker runs again. The `signature` is `UNIQUE` on the transfer record once
   it is present.

This flow is deliberately low-level. SDP provides no session object. Treat the `orders` table as
your checkout state machine, and treat SDP as the settlement and status backend.

## Related

- [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification). What each status means, and when a
  payment is safe to act on.
- [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing). List inbound transfers,
  deduplicate them, and build a delta-poll worker.

### Verifying a payment
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/accept-verification

> What each transfer status means, what finality means on Solana, and how often to poll.

When a payment lands on a wallet you control, the inbound transfer moves through a small set of
statuses. This page describes those statuses. It explains what each one says about finality on
Solana, and how to decide when it is safe to ship goods or release funds.

## Status lifecycle

The `status` field on the `Transfer` record takes one of several values. The set of values depends
on whether the record is a wallet transfer or a ramp transfer.

**Wallet transfers.** These come from `POST /v1/payments/transfers`, and from inbound transfers
that SDP discovers onchain.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `processing` | The transfer is in flight. This is the initial state of an outbound transfer at record creation. SDP is building and submitting the transaction. `signature` is not set yet. |
| `confirmed` | The cluster confirmed the transaction. `signature` and `slot` are set. `blockTime` can also be set, but it is not guaranteed at this stage. Treat it as optional until the transfer is `finalized`. |
| `finalized` | The slot that holds the transaction is locked in. This is the strongest guarantee the Solana cluster offers, and it is safe to treat as irreversible. `signature` and `slot` are set. `blockTime` is best-effort, and it can stay `null` for a transfer that the `track-pending-transfers` job finalizes. That job updates the status and the slot, but it does not backfill the block time. Resolve a definitive timestamp from `signature` through Solana RPC if you need one. |
| `failed` | SDP built and submitted the transaction, and the network rejected it. Common causes are insufficient funds, a frozen account, and an expired blockhash. The `error` field describes what reached the chain. |

An outbound wallet transfer moves from `processing` to `confirmed` to `finalized`. An inbound
transfer that SDP discovers through onchain signature history appears directly at `confirmed`, or
at `failed`. An inbound transfer never appears as `processing`.

**Ramp transfers.** A [Ramp Quote](/docs/payments/ramps) creates these.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `pending` | SDP created the quote. No funding has been detected yet, and there is no `signature`. |
| `awaiting_payment` | The quote's delivery mode is `manual_instructions`. SDP is waiting for the payer to fund the account described in the quote. |
| `settling` | The provider detected the payment, or started to process it. |
| `completed` | The provider reports that the ramp settled. |
| `canceled` | You canceled the transfer with `POST /v1/payments/ramps/transfers/cancel` before it was funded. |
| `expired` | The funding window elapsed and no payment arrived. |
| `failed` | The provider rejected or reversed the ramp. The `error` field describes why, when SDP sets it. |

Any state can move to `failed`. The terminal states are `failed`, `completed`, `canceled`, and
`expired`.

## Finality on Solana

For real-money flows, treat `finalized` as the safe-to-act-on signal.

`confirmed` is durable enough for most workflows that are not adversarial, such as showing a paid
badge in your own dashboard. A large enough cluster reorganization can in theory roll back a
`confirmed` transaction. This does not happen to a `finalized` transaction.

Use `confirmed` to release low-stakes side effects, such as a status email or a screen update. Use
`finalized` for irreversible side effects, such as releasing custody, shipping high-value goods, or
posting to your general ledger.

## Polling cadence

SDP does not emit settlement webhooks today. You observe a status by polling:

- `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{id}` returns the current state of one transfer.
- `GET /v1/payments/transfers?direction=inbound&from=…` returns a windowed list. See
  [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing).

The right cadence depends on how quickly you need to see a state change, and on how large your
retry budget is. These ranges are a reasonable starting point:

- **Active checkout**, where the customer is watching a payment screen. Poll every 2 to 5 seconds
  for up to a minute, then back off.
- **Background reconciliation**, where nobody is waiting. Poll every 15 to 30 seconds, or on each
  worker tick.
- **Long-tail catch-up**, where you read a status after the fact. Read once when your application
  needs to act. Do not run a polling loop.

The backend team plans to tighten these numbers once it confirms a target. Treat the ranges above
as defensible defaults today.

## Independent verification

Every transfer that reaches `processing` or a later state carries enough information to verify
against the network directly:

- **`signature`** is the Solana transaction signature. Paste it into [Solscan](https://solscan.io/)
  or [Solana Explorer](https://explorer.solana.com/) to see the onchain record.
- **`slot`** is the slot that the transaction landed in.
- **`blockTime`** is the ISO 8601 timestamp of slot finality.
- **`fee`** is the fee paid, in lamports.

If you run your own indexer with `getSignatureStatuses` against a Solana RPC endpoint,
cross-reference the SDP `signature` against your indexer. That confirms that the SDP status matches
what your own nodes see.

## Risk metadata

When a risk-screening provider is configured on the organization, a transfer can carry a `risk`
field. That field holds `provider`, `score`, `level`, and `evaluatedAt`. The `level` value is
`low`, `medium`, `high`, or `unknown`. Use it to gate downstream side effects on a risk threshold.
The field is absent when no risk provider is configured.

Risk evaluation does not block a transfer by default. A transfer can complete with a high risk
score. To halt a transfer at a risk threshold, enforce that in your own application logic on top of
the `risk.level` value.

## Failure handling

When `status` settles to `failed`:

- Read the `error` field. SDP returns the chain-level error message. Common causes are insufficient
  funds on the source wallet, an account frozen by the token authority, and a stale blockhash.
- Decide whether to retry. The original transfer record is terminal. A retry creates a new transfer
  with a new ID, and eventually a new signature.
- Report the failure to whoever needs to know, such as the merchant, the customer, or your
  operations team.

## Related

- [Accept payments](/docs/payments/accept-overview). The wider inbound-payment flow.
- [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing). Status checks across many
  transfers, from one list call.
- [How payments work on SDP](/docs/payments/concepts#the-transfer-data-model). The full field
  reference for a transfer.

### Indexing and reconciliation
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/accept-indexing

> List inbound transfers, paginate them, deduplicate them, and reconcile them against your ledger.

`GET /v1/payments/transfers` is the main endpoint for reconciliation. By default it returns
paginated, persisted transfer records across your organization's custody wallets.

It filters on direction, status, token, exact `custodyWalletId`, and date range. Use it to mirror
SDP transfers locally, to match an inbound payment to an order, and to drive a delta-polling
worker.

To include recent onchain observations for one exact wallet, set `custodyWalletId` and
`includeObserved=true`.

## Listing inbound transfers

This is the smallest inbound-only request.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers?direction=inbound&pageSize=50" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="list-inbound-transfers.ts"
const url = new URL("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers");
url.searchParams.set("direction", "inbound");
url.searchParams.set("pageSize", "50");

const res = await fetch(url, {
  headers: { Authorization: "Bearer sk_test_..." },
});
const { data, meta } = await res.json();
// data: Transfer[]
// meta: { total, page, pageSize, hasMore, requestId }
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

### Query parameters

| Parameter | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `direction` | `inbound` \| `outbound` | The common filter. `inbound` means payments to wallets you control. |
| `status` | `pending` \| `processing` \| `confirmed` \| `finalized` \| `failed` | Scope the list to a single state. |
| `custodyWalletId` | string | An exact SDP wallet ID. `GET /v1/wallets` returns it as `id`. |
| `includeObserved` | boolean | Default `false`. When `true`, SDP adds recent onchain activity for the exact `custodyWalletId`. You cannot use it without that filter. A synthetic observed row has `custodyWalletId: null`. |
| `token` | string | Filter by token symbol or by onchain mint address. SDP matches it exactly against the stored `token` value on the transfer. |
| `from`, `to` | ISO 8601 datetime | A time-window filter on `createdAt`. Pass an ISO 8601 timestamp, such as `2026-05-14T00:00:00Z`. The trailing `Z` means UTC. |
| `page` | integer | Default `1`. |
| `pageSize` | integer | Default `20`, maximum `100`. |

## Deduplication

A transfer has two natural keys for this.

1. **`Transfer.id`** is SDP-internal and immutable. It is present on every transfer, including a
   `pending` one that has no signature yet. Use it as your local primary key.
2. **`Transfer.signature`** is the onchain signature. SDP sets it once it has built the transaction
   and observed it onchain. That is usually at `confirmed` or `finalized`, but treat the presence
   of the value as the trigger rather than the status. A `processing` record, and even a `pending`
   record, can still have a null signature. The column is `UNIQUE` across the SDP transfers table
   wherever it is set, so two records cannot share a signature. Use it when you need to
   deduplicate across several data sources, such as SDP plus a parallel chain indexer, and only
   once `signature` is present.

In practice: store transfers in your reconciliation table keyed by the SDP `Transfer.id`, and
assert that `signature` is unique once it is populated.

## Reconciling an order

SDP does not populate `Transfer.memo` for a customer-initiated inbound transfer, because SDP does
not extract memo-program instructions into that field. The inbound record also carries no reference
field.

The reliable correlation key on the record is therefore the inbound transfer's `destination`. Match
it against an order whose pre-issued receiving address is that same `destination`.

The typical inbound match cycle runs like this.

1. **Read** recent persisted inbound transfers for the token you care about:
   ```text title="Request"
   GET /v1/payments/transfers
     ?direction=inbound
     &token=<mint or SOL>
     &from=<since last reconciled>
     &to=<now>
     &pageSize=100
   ```
2. **For each transfer**, look up an open order keyed by the transfer's `destination`, with
   `findOrderByDestination(tr.destination)`.
3. **If it matches**, check that the amount and the token match the values on the order row. Then
   mark the order paid, record the SDP `Transfer.id`, and dispatch the downstream side effects,
   such as an email, a shipment, or a ledger entry.
4. **If it does not match**, leave the transfer for the next pass. It can be an early arrival for
   an order you have not staged yet. Flag it for manual review after a grace window.

If you need correlation by memo or by Solana Pay `reference`, for example in a single-wallet flow
where many orders share one destination address, read the onchain transaction through Solana RPC
using the transfer's `signature`.

## Solana Pay reference accounts (roadmap)

SDP does not attach a Solana Pay reference pubkey onchain, and an inbound transfer record does not
expose a reference field today. That leaves two realistic correlation options.

- **Per-order destination addresses.** Pre-issue a fresh receiving wallet for each order and match
  on `Transfer.destination`. This is the recommended pattern. See
  [Reconciling an order](#reconciling-an-order) above.
- **Onchain reads through Solana RPC**, keyed off the transfer's `signature`. Use these to recover
  the memo-program instruction or the Solana Pay `reference` that the transfer record does not
  carry.

## A delta-poll worker

This reconciliation worker wakes on a tick and asks what is new since the last tick.

<Tabs items={["TypeScript"]}>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="reconcile-tick.ts"
const OVERLAP_MS = 5_000; // re-query the last 5s on each tick to catch boundary arrivals

async function reconcileTick(state: WorkerState) {
  // Nudge `from` backwards by the overlap window; `alreadySeen` dedupes the
  // resulting duplicates. Always advance the high-water mark to `to` regardless,
  // otherwise the window grows without bound.
  const fromMs = state.lastSeenIso
    ? Date.parse(state.lastSeenIso) - OVERLAP_MS
    : Date.now() - 60_000;
  const from = new Date(fromMs).toISOString();
  const to = new Date().toISOString();

  // This lists persisted records. To discover additional recent chain activity,
  // run the same window per exact wallet with custodyWalletId + includeObserved.
  for await (const tr of listInbound({ from, to })) {
    if (await alreadySeen(tr.id)) continue;

    // Match by destination — the on-record correlation key for inbound transfers.
    // `tr.memo` is omitted (undefined) for customer-initiated inbound payments.
    const order = await findOrderByDestination(tr.destination);
    if (!order) {
      await persistUnmatched(tr);
      continue;
    }

    if (tr.status === "finalized") {
      await markOrderPaid(order, tr);
    }
    await persistSeen(tr.id, tr.status);
  }

  state.lastSeenIso = to;
}
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Notes:

- The overlap window, 5 seconds above, re-queries the trailing edge of the last tick. It catches a
  transfer that arrives at the boundary, and `alreadySeen` collapses the duplicates that result.
- The high-water mark advances to `to` on every pass, even though `from` rolls back. Otherwise the
  query window grows without bound.
- Always re-fetch a transfer to upgrade its status. A transfer seen as `confirmed` on one tick
  appears as `finalized` on a later tick.
- Use `pageSize=100` and the async iterator pattern to handle a large window. See
  [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts).

## Related

- [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification). Status reads for a single transfer.
- [Accept payments](/docs/payments/accept-overview). The wider inbound flow.
- [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts). The same list endpoint, used outbound.
- [Payments API reference](/docs/reference/api/payments). The full endpoint reference.

---

## Payments — Ramps

### Ramps
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/ramps

> Discover corridors, price a Ramp Quote, and hand the user to the ramp provider's own flow.

SDP puts every ramp provider behind a single pricing step called a **Ramp Quote**. SDP prices the
quote against the provider at the moment you request it.

There is no execute endpoint. SDP creates the quote and hands the end user to the provider's own
flow, either a hosted redirect or a set of funding instructions.

Every quote is tied to a **Counterparty** and to a custody wallet you control. The counterparty is
the KYC subject for the ramp. For per-provider configuration, see
[Ramp providers](/docs/payments/ramps-providers).

## Prerequisites

1. **A counterparty.** Create one with `POST /v1/counterparties` before you request a quote.
2. **Provider requirements satisfied**, when the provider needs them. Some providers require KYC
   details or bank details collected against the counterparty before they price or accept a quote.
   Check `GET /v1/counterparties/{counterpartyId}/requirements?provider=…&direction=…`. Submit the
   collected fields with `POST` to the same path until `status` reads `ready`.
3. **A custody wallet you control.** It is the crypto leg: the onramp destination, or the offramp
   source.

## Discovering corridors

`GET /v1/payments/ramps/onramp/currency` and `GET /v1/payments/ramps/offramp/currency` list the
fiat and crypto pairs that SDP supports, and which providers cover each pair. They return the
corridor dimensions: currency, country coverage, and entity type.

<Tabs items={["curl"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/onramp/currency?source=USD&dest=usdc.solana" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

| Query param | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `source` | Onramp: the fiat currency, as an ISO code. Offramp: the asset rail, such as `usdc.solana` or `sol.solana`. |
| `dest` | Onramp: the asset rail. Offramp: the fiat currency. |
| `provider` | Narrow the result to one provider. |

The `pairs` list in the response says which providers cover each source and destination
combination. The `providerDetails` object gives each provider's country coverage and its supported
entity types for that direction.

## Estimating a rate

`POST /v1/payments/ramps/onramp/estimate` and `POST /v1/payments/ramps/offramp/estimate` return a
rate preview. They create nothing, and they need no counterparty and no wallet.

SDP calls every provider on the corridor at the same time, and returns one result per provider.
Each result is `ok` and carries the estimate, or it is `unsupported`, or it is `error`.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/onramp/estimate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "assetRail": "usdc.solana",
    "fiatCurrency": "USD",
    "fiatAmount": "100.00"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="estimate-onramp.ts"
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/onramp/estimate",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      assetRail: "usdc.solana",
      fiatCurrency: "USD",
      fiatAmount: "100.00",
    }),
  }
);
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.estimates — one entry per provider on the corridor
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Each entry under `estimates` carries `fiatAmount`, `cryptoAmount`, `exchangeRate`, and `fees` when
its `status` is `ok`. Use it to show the user a rate before they commit to a quote.

## Requesting a quote

`POST /v1/payments/ramps/onramp/quote` goes from fiat to crypto.
`POST /v1/payments/ramps/offramp/quote` goes from crypto to fiat. Both create the actual **Ramp
Quote** against the provider you name.

This is the step that talks to the provider. For most providers it also creates a record on the
provider's side. Unlike an estimate, it requires a resolved counterparty and a resolved wallet.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/onramp/quote \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "provider": "moonpay",
    "counterpartyId": "cp_...",
    "destinationCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_...",
    "assetRail": "usdc.solana",
    "fiatCurrency": "USD",
    "fiatAmount": "100.00"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="onramp-quote.ts"
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/onramp/quote",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      provider: "moonpay",
      counterpartyId: "cp_...",
      destinationCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_...",
      assetRail: "usdc.solana",
      fiatCurrency: "USD",
      fiatAmount: "100.00",
    }),
  }
);
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.quote.deliveryMode tells you what to do next — see below
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="OnrampQuote.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/onramp/quote"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        {
          "provider": "moonpay",
          "counterpartyId": "cp_...",
          "destinationCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_...",
          "assetRail": "usdc.solana",
          "fiatCurrency": "USD",
          "fiatAmount": "100.00"
        }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

### Request fields

| Field | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `provider` | yes | One of `moonpay`, `lightspark`, `bvnk`, `moneygram`, `coinbase`, `mural`, `stripe`. `moneygram` works in sandbox only. `coinbase` accepts a quote in sandbox only. |
| `counterpartyId` | yes | An existing counterparty. SDP resolves the provider-side customer and payout-account state from it on the server. You do not pass that state on the request. A counterparty stores no identity fields and no email field. |
| `destinationCustodyWalletId` (onramp) / `sourceCustodyWalletId` (offramp) | yes | A custody wallet you control, given by the `id` that `GET /v1/wallets` returns. SDP resolves it against the wallet scope of your API key. The shape is the same for every provider. |
| `assetRail` | yes | The canonical SDP asset rail, such as `usdc.solana`, `usdt.solana`, or `sol.solana`. |
| `fiatCurrency` | onramp: yes; offramp: conditional | Required for every onramp, and for a Lightspark or BVNK offramp. A provider that resolves the fiat currency inside its own flow, such as MoneyGram, can omit it on an offramp. |
| `fiatAmount` (onramp) / `cryptoAmount` (offramp) | yes | A decimal string greater than zero. |
| `rampsMemo` | no | Up to 20 key and value string pairs. SDP stores them on the resulting transfer for your own correlation. |

The quote also creates the underlying **Payment Transfer** record for the ramp. Log the returned
`quote.id`, which is the transfer's `providerReference`, for your own records.

### Delivery mode

`quote.deliveryMode` tells you how to complete the flow with the provider you named.

| Provider | `deliveryMode` | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MoonPay | `hosted` | Redirect the user to `quote.hostedUrl`. |
| Lightspark | `manual_instructions` | Display the funding instructions in `quote.paymentInstructions`. They hold the bank or wallet details to send fiat to. |
| BVNK | `manual_instructions` | Display `quote.paymentInstructions`, as with Lightspark. |
| MoneyGram | `session_widget` | Mount `quote.widgetUrl` with `quote.sessionToken`. Onramp and offramp both work this way, in sandbox only. |
| Coinbase | `hosted` | Redirect the user to `quote.hostedUrl`. Onramp only, and quote creation works in sandbox only today. |
| Mural | `manual_instructions` | Display `quote.paymentInstructions`. Onramp only. |
| Stripe | `session_widget` | Mount the session with `quote.clientSecret` and `quote.publishableKey`. Onramp only. |

There is no further SDP endpoint to call after this step. The provider owns settlement from here.

Watch for the resulting onchain transfer on the destination wallet with
[`GET /v1/payments/transfers?direction=inbound`](/docs/payments/accept-indexing). For an offramp
payout, watch the provider's own dashboard or webhook for the settlement confirmation.

## Canceling a quote

`POST /v1/payments/ramps/transfers/cancel` cancels the transfer behind a quote while that transfer
is still `pending` or `awaiting_payment`, which means before the provider has moved money.

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/transfers/cancel \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "provider": "bvnk",
    "providerReference": "..."
  }'
```

A transfer past that window, one that is already funded or settling, returns an error instead of
canceling.

## Status field

`quote.status` is one of `pending`, `processing`, `completed`, and `failed`. It reflects the state
that the provider reported at the moment SDP created the quote.

SDP does not poll the provider afterwards to refresh that value, and there is no read endpoint for
the quote itself. For the onchain side of a successful onramp, observe the resulting inbound
transfer on the destination wallet. See [Accept payments](/docs/payments/accept-overview).

## Rate limits

Estimate calls and quote calls carry fail-closed quotas. An estimate fans out one live call per
provider on the corridor, and a quote creates a record on the provider's side.

| Endpoint | Per-key limit | Per-organization limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.../estimate` | 30 / minute | 120 / minute |
| `.../quote` | 20 / minute | 60 / minute |

## Provider selection

You always pass `provider` explicitly. SDP does not choose one for you. Choose on three points.

- **Coverage.** Which providers your organization can use. See
  [Provider gating](/docs/payments/ramps-providers#provider-gating).
- **Corridor.** The currency, the country, and the entity type. Check them with the
  currency-discovery endpoints above.
- **Sandbox needs.** SDP chooses sandbox or production per request, from the environment of the
  calling API key. See
  [Sandbox vs production selection](/docs/payments/ramps-providers#sandbox-vs-production-selection).

## Fiat currency support

Fiat currency support is specific to a corridor. It is not a fixed allowlist. Call
`GET /v1/payments/ramps/onramp/currency` and `GET /v1/payments/ramps/offramp/currency` to see
which fiat currencies a given provider covers for a given asset rail.

## Related

- [Ramp providers](/docs/payments/ramps-providers). Per-provider configuration and the capability
  matrix.
- [Accept payments](/docs/payments/accept-overview). How an onramp delivery appears as an inbound
  transfer.
- [Provider onboarding](/docs/reference/provider-onboarding) — how providers are activated for an
  organization.

---

### Ramp providers
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/ramps-providers

> The capability matrix, the credentials, and the per-provider notes for the seven SDP ramp providers.

SDP integrates seven ramp providers: MoonPay, Lightspark, BVNK, MoneyGram, Coinbase, Mural, and
Stripe.

An administrator configures each provider with credentials on the SDP API deployment. Each
organization is then entitled to some or all of the configured providers. See
[Provider gating](#provider-gating).

The same `provider` string on `POST /v1/payments/ramps/onramp/quote` and
`POST /v1/payments/ramps/offramp/quote` selects between them.

## Sandbox vs production selection

SDP chooses the sandbox mode or the production mode per request, not at deployment time.

- A deployment that is not a production deployment always uses the sandbox credentials.
- On a production deployment, the environment of the calling API key picks the mode. An `sk_test_`
  key uses sandbox. An `sk_live_` key uses production.

Configure both credential pairs for any provider that you want to serve test traffic and live
traffic on the same deployment. MoonPay, Lightspark, BVNK, and Mural each read a separate sandbox
pair and production pair this way.

Coinbase and Stripe use a single credential pair, whichever mode SDP resolves. See their sections
below. MoneyGram has sandbox credentials only today.

## Capability matrix

| Provider | Onramp | Offramp | Sandbox | Delivery mode | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MoonPay | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | `hosted` | SDP selects sandbox or production per request. See [Sandbox vs production selection](#sandbox-vs-production-selection). |
| Lightspark | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | `manual_instructions` | Grid API. The same per-request sandbox and production selection as MoonPay. |
| BVNK | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | `manual_instructions` | Hawk authentication. SDP builds the compliance party details from the counterparty record, not from the request. |
| MoneyGram | ✓ (sandbox only) | ✓ (sandbox only) | ✓ | `session_widget` | A sandbox-only pilot integration. There is no production credential path yet. |
| Coinbase | ✓ (sandbox only) | ✗ | ✓ | `hosted` | Onramp only. Rate estimates work in production. Order creation works in sandbox only. |
| Mural | ✓ | Estimate only | ✓ | `manual_instructions` | Onramp only for a quote. The offramp rate estimate works, and offramp quote creation is not implemented yet. |
| Stripe | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ (shared credentials) | `session_widget` | Onramp only. There are no separate sandbox credentials. Supply a Stripe test-mode secret key. |

## MoonPay

| Variable | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MOONPAY_API_KEY` | For a production request | Production API key. |
| `MOONPAY_SECRET_KEY` | For a production request | Production secret. SDP signs the onramp and offramp URLs with it. Pair it with `MOONPAY_API_KEY`. |
| `MOONPAY_SANDBOX_API_KEY` | For a sandbox request | Sandbox API key. |
| `MOONPAY_SANDBOX_SECRET_KEY` | For a sandbox request | Sandbox secret. Pair it with `MOONPAY_SANDBOX_API_KEY`. |
| `MOONPAY_ONRAMP_URL` | Never | Overrides the onramp host. It defaults to MoonPay's standard URLs. The sandbox or production choice follows the [per-request rule](#sandbox-vs-production-selection). |
| `MOONPAY_OFFRAMP_URL` | Never | The same override for the offramp host. |

MoonPay normalizes its own currency codes internally. SDP accepts the canonical asset rails, such
as `usdc.solana`, and maps them to MoonPay's code, such as `usdc_sol`.

## Lightspark

| Variable | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LIGHTSPARK_GRID_CLIENT_ID` | For a production request | Production Grid API client identifier. |
| `LIGHTSPARK_GRID_CLIENT_SECRET` | For a production request | Production Grid API client secret. |
| `LIGHTSPARK_GRID_SANDBOX_CLIENT_ID` | For a sandbox request | Sandbox Grid API client identifier. |
| `LIGHTSPARK_GRID_SANDBOX_CLIENT_SECRET` | For a sandbox request | Sandbox Grid API client secret. |

SDP integrates Lightspark against the Grid API at
`https://api.lightspark.com/grid/2025-10-13`. The sandbox or production choice follows the
[per-request rule](#sandbox-vs-production-selection).

`destinationCustodyWalletId` and `sourceCustodyWalletId` are your own custody wallet, as with
every other provider. SDP resolves the Lightspark customer ID and payout account on the server,
from the counterparty's provider requirements. You do not pass them on the quote request.

A counterparty no longer stores identity fields or an email field. An existing Lightspark customer
still resolves from the provider data. Creating a first-time customer currently fails with a clear
error, until just-in-time identity collection is connected.

A Lightspark quote always returns `deliveryMode: "manual_instructions"`. The response carries
funding instructions to display to the payer, not a redirect URL.

## BVNK

| Variable | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `BVNK_WALLET_ID` | For a production request | Production BVNK-side wallet used for settlement. |
| `BVNK_HAWK_AUTH_ID` | For a production request | Production Hawk auth id. Pair it with `BVNK_HAWK_SECRET_KEY`. |
| `BVNK_HAWK_SECRET_KEY` | For a production request | Production Hawk secret key. |
| `BVNK_SANDBOX_WALLET_ID` | For a sandbox request | Sandbox BVNK wallet. |
| `BVNK_SANDBOX_HAWK_AUTH_ID` | For a sandbox request | Sandbox Hawk auth id. |
| `BVNK_SANDBOX_HAWK_SECRET_KEY` | For a sandbox request | Sandbox Hawk secret key. |

BVNK uses Hawk authentication. SDP does not support bearer-token authentication for BVNK.

BVNK shares travel-rule and compliance data, so it requires party details such as a name and an
address. A counterparty no longer stores those fields. Customer creation, payment-rule creation,
and the offramp compliance payload therefore fail today with a clear error, at the seam where
just-in-time collection will go.

A BVNK quote always returns `deliveryMode: "manual_instructions"`. The response carries
funding-account details to display to the payer.

## MoneyGram

| Variable | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MONEYGRAM_SANDBOX_PUBLIC_KEY` | For every MoneyGram request | Sandbox public key. SDP sends it as `x-api-key` on the asset-rail discovery call that lists currencies. |
| `MONEYGRAM_SANDBOX_SECRET_KEY` | For every MoneyGram request | Sandbox secret key. SDP sends it as `x-api-key` on the estimate, quote, and session calls. |

MoneyGram is a sandbox-only pilot integration today. The client always calls MoneyGram's sandbox
host, and it throws an error when a request resolves to production. There is no production
credential pair to configure yet.

A MoneyGram quote always returns `deliveryMode: "session_widget"`. Onramp and offramp both create
a session against the same endpoint. Both return a `widgetUrl`, with `mode=on-ramp` or
`mode=off-ramp`, and a short-lived `sessionToken` to mount.

MoneyGram needs no provider requirements collection. SDP treats every counterparty as ready.

## Coinbase

| Variable | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `COINBASE_CDP_API_KEY_ID` | For every Coinbase request | CDP Secret API Key id. SDP uses the same key for sandbox and for production. Sandbox is flagged per request, not by a separate credential. |
| `COINBASE_CDP_API_KEY_SECRET` | For every Coinbase request | CDP Secret API Key secret. Pair it with `COINBASE_CDP_API_KEY_ID`. SDP signs a per-request JWT with it. |

Coinbase is onramp-only. Both `estimateOfframp` and `createOfframpQuote` reject the call with
"Coinbase Onramp does not support off-ramp."

A Coinbase onramp quote always returns `deliveryMode: "hosted"`. SDP creates a guest-checkout
Apple Pay order and returns its payment link as `hostedUrl`.

Order creation, which is the quote step, works in sandbox only today. It requires a buyer
agreement and phone-OTP attestation timestamps that the SDP production flow does not collect yet.
A non-sandbox request therefore fails loudly, rather than sending a false attestation. Rate
estimates carry no such restriction, and they work in both modes.

Coinbase also requires an email value and a phone value. Quote creation currently fails at the
seam where just-in-time collection will go.

## Mural

| Variable | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MURAL_PAY_API_KEY` | For a production request | Production API key for the organization, account, and payin calls. |
| `MURAL_PAY_SANDBOX_API_KEY` | For a sandbox request | The sandbox equivalent. |
| `MURAL_PAY_TRANSFER_API_KEY` | For a production request | Production transfer-scoped key. SDP sends it as a separate header on payout-execute calls. |
| `MURAL_PAY_SANDBOX_TRANSFER_API_KEY` | For a sandbox request | The sandbox equivalent of the transfer key. |

Mural onramp accepts a business counterparty only. It does not accept the individual entity type.

A Mural quote requires that the counterparty's Mural organization and payin account already exist.
You create them through provider requirements onboarding, which covers organization creation,
terms-of-service acceptance, and verification.

The quote returns `deliveryMode: "manual_instructions"`, built from that account's active payin
method. The quote step itself makes no live call to Mural.

An existing Mural organization still resolves from the provider data. Creating a first-time
organization currently fails with a clear error, until just-in-time identity collection is
connected.

Offramp rate estimates work today, through a real call to Mural's fees endpoint. Offramp quote
creation always throws, because it is not implemented yet.

## Stripe

| Variable | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` | For every Stripe request | Secret key. SDP sends it as the username on HTTP Basic authentication. One key serves both modes. Use an `sk_test_…` key for sandbox and an `sk_live_…` key for production. |
| `STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` | For every Stripe request | Publishable key. SDP echoes it back on the quote, so that your client can mount the onramp session. |

Stripe is onramp-only. Both `estimateOfframp` and `createOfframpQuote` reject the call as
unsupported. Stripe onramp also accepts only `usdc.solana` and `sol.solana` as destination assets.

A Stripe quote always returns `deliveryMode: "session_widget"`. It carries a `clientSecret` and a
`publishableKey` to mount Stripe's crypto onramp session, plus an optional `redirectUrl`.

## Provider gating

An organization can be restricted to a subset of providers, even when the credentials for all
seven are populated. This is
[**Provider Availability**](/docs/reference/provider-onboarding): a provider must be configured
for the deployment and either generally available or manually activated for the organization.

SDP checks this on every ramp call. When the organization does not have availability for the
requested provider, the call returns an error.

To activate or change provider availability for a deployment, see
[Provider onboarding](/docs/reference/provider-onboarding).

## Choosing a provider

| Need | Lean towards |
| --- | --- |
| Fastest sandbox iteration | MoonPay or BVNK. |
| Travel-rule and compliance party metadata | BVNK. |
| Lightning-aware fiat settlement | Lightspark. |
| Broadest payment-method coverage | MoonPay, depending on the corridor. |
| Business-entity onramp counterparties | Mural, its only supported entity type. |
| An onramp UI embedded as a widget or session | MoneyGram, in sandbox only, or Stripe. |
| Onramp only, with no offramp | Coinbase or Stripe. |

For self-hosted deployments where only a subset of providers will ever be configured, see
[Providers optional for self-hosted SDP](/docs/reference/provider-onboarding) — SDP supports
running with any single provider active.

## Related

- [Ramps](/docs/payments/ramps). The onramp and offramp endpoints, and the request shape.
- [Provider onboarding](/docs/reference/provider-onboarding) — activation flow.
