## Tutorials

### Issue a regulated stablecoin
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/tutorials/issue-a-regulated-stablecoin

> Issue a stablecoin on Solana with institutional custody, address screening, and the freeze, seize, and burn controls a regulator expects.

This tutorial shows you how to issue a regulated stablecoin on Solana. The result is a token that a
bank's compliance committee and a federal examiner can review.

Issuing a regulated stablecoin is not the same as deploying a token. It requires institutional
custody, integrated compliance, and reversible operations from the first day. The
[GENIUS Act](https://www.gibsondunn.com/the-genius-act-a-new-era-of-stablecoin-regulation/) treats
those capabilities as preconditions, not as features.

The authors ran every code sample in this tutorial against the SDP sandbox in September 2026. The
request and response shapes below are what the API returned.

## 1. What a regulated stablecoin requires

This tutorial assumes that you are a developer at a financial institution or a fintech, and that
you work under a compliance officer's review. That officer sees the decisions you make here.

Three conditions shape every step that follows.

**A federally chartered custodian holds the signing keys.** A regulated stablecoin is not held on
an engineer's laptop. For a US issuer operating under the GENIUS Act framework, the custodian is
usually Anchorage Digital Bank or an equivalent federally chartered crypto bank. The custodian
holds the keys for the mint, freeze, and permanent-delegate authorities.

**Compliance is integrated from the first day.** SDP screens every transfer destination before it
builds the transfer. Every frozen account ties back to a court order, a sanctions notice, or an
internal compliance ticket. The screening endpoints sit in the same API as the mint and burn
endpoints.

**Freeze, seize, and force-burn are required capabilities.** The GENIUS Act requires you to have
them ready before launch. They exist in the SDP API because the regulation requires them, and your
compliance officer checks for them. Section 5 covers each one in detail.

## 2. Prerequisites

You need the following before you start. Expect about thirty minutes if you have none of them
today.

- An SDP account and an organization.
- A configured custody provider.
- Two project-scoped API keys. One is for routine operations. One is for compliance operations.
- A funded devnet wallet.

### Account and organization

Sign up at [platform.solana.com](https://platform.solana.com) with email, Google, or GitHub. Create
your organization when the dashboard prompts you.

SDP provisions a matching organization on its side through a [Clerk](https://clerk.com) webhook.
The dashboard's onboarding cards clear once that sync lands.

### Custody provider

An institutional issuer in the US pipeline configures
[Anchorage Digital Bank](https://www.anchorage.com/platform/stablecoin-issuance) as the custodian.
Anchorage is not entitled by default, so an administrator must have access granted to your
organization first. The Anchorage onboarding team then provisions the signing wallets and binds
them to your SDP organization.

If you work on the self-serve sandbox without an Anchorage relationship, SDP provisions Privy
wallets for development access instead. The API is identical. Only the `provider` field on the
wallet record differs.

### Mint the two project-scoped API keys

The dashboard's **Create API key** dialog creates organization-scoped keys only. The issuance API
requires project-scoped keys. Project management in the dashboard is on the SDP roadmap. Until it
lands, use a short sequence of API calls instead.

<Steps>

<Step>

From the dashboard, mint an organization-scoped API key with **Role: Admin** and
**Environment: Sandbox**. This is your bootstrap credential.

![Create API key dialog in the SDP dashboard, with Role set to Admin and Environment set to Sandbox.](/issue-a-regulated-stablecoin/01-create-api-key-dialog.png)

</Step>

<Step>

With the Admin key, call `GET /v1/projects`. Pick the project with the slug `default-sandbox`.

SDP provisions every organization with exactly one sandbox project and one production project.
Isolation between workloads comes from separate organizations, not from additional projects. The
next step needs the project ID.

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "projects": [
      {
        "id": "prj_3bc13bcb-...",
        "slug": "default-sandbox",
        "environment": "sandbox",
        "status": "active"
      },
      {
        "id": "prj_8a201d47-...",
        "slug": "default-production",
        "environment": "production",
        "status": "active"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

</Step>

<Step>

Call `POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/api-keys` twice to mint two project-scoped keys.

Give the first key `role: "api_developer"`. You use it for routine create, mint, and burn calls.
Give the second key `role: "api_admin"`. You use it for compliance operations: screening, freeze,
seize, and force-burn.

Each response includes the full key value exactly once:

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "apiKey": {
      "id": "key_375fe1e1-...",
      "keyPrefix": "sk_test__b3",
      "key": "sk_test_<full key, shown once>",
      "role": "api_developer",
      "environment": "sandbox"
    }
  }
}
```

<Callout type="warn">
The `key` field appears only on this response. Copy it into your secrets manager immediately. SDP
does not return it again.
</Callout>

</Step>

</Steps>

Store the two project-scoped keys with your other production secrets. Keep the organization-scoped
Admin key cold. You touch it only when you provision more keys or rotate them.

### Fund your custody wallet on devnet

On devnet, the custody wallet starts at zero lamports. SDP cannot pay transaction fees from an
empty wallet. Fund it from the browser faucet:

<Steps>

<Step>
Go to [faucet.solana.com](https://faucet.solana.com).
</Step>

<Step>
Set the network to **Devnet**.
</Step>

<Step>
Enter the wallet's public key.
</Step>

<Step>
Request one SOL.
</Step>

</Steps>

The browser faucet is more reliable than the RPC `requestAirdrop` method, which is rate-limited
heavily. Production readers operating under Anchorage do not do this step. The bank funds the
custody address as part of its standard operational support.

### API base URL

The SDP API base URL is `https://api.solana.com`. Every request in this tutorial uses this
hostname, in sandbox and in production.

### Configure your client and verify the setup

Configure two HTTP clients, one per project-scoped key, with a thin wrapper around `fetch`.

Every state-mutating execute endpoint in SDP supports an `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header. Those
endpoints are deploy, mint, burn, seize, force-burn, and authority. A retry with the same key
replays the original response. A retry with a different key is a new request. The header is what
makes network-level retries safe under partial failure, so the client below sends it.

```javascript title="sdp-client.js"
const BASE = "https://api.solana.com";

class SdpClient {
  constructor(apiKey, baseUrl = BASE) {
    this.apiKey = apiKey;
    this.baseUrl = baseUrl;
  }

  async request(method, path, body, { idempotencyKey } = {}) {
    const headers = {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${this.apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    };
    if (idempotencyKey) headers["Idempotency-Key"] = idempotencyKey;

    const res = await fetch(`${this.baseUrl}${path}`, {
      method,
      headers,
      body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
    });
    const payload = await res.json();
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${payload.error.code}: ${payload.error.message}`);
    return payload;
  }

  get(path) { return this.request("GET", path); }
  post(path, body, opts) { return this.request("POST", path, body, opts); }
}

const sdp = new SdpClient(process.env.SDP_API_KEY);
const sdpAdmin = new SdpClient(process.env.SDP_ADMIN_API_KEY);
const idempotencyKey = (op) => `${op}-${crypto.randomUUID()}`;
```

Use `sdp` for routine operations: create, mint, and burn. Use `sdpAdmin` for compliance operations:
screening, freeze, seize, and force-burn.

Generate one idempotency key per logical operation, not per retry. Create the key once before the
first attempt. Store it in a variable, and reuse that same value for every retry of the same call.

Now confirm the setup. List the wallets bound to your project:

```javascript title="list-wallets.js"
const { data } = await sdp.get("/v1/wallets");
const custodyWallet = data.wallets.find(
  (wallet) => wallet.status === "active" && wallet.isRuntimeExecutionAllowed
);
if (!custodyWallet) throw new Error("No active custody wallet can execute");

const signingCustodyWalletId = custodyWallet.id;
const custodyAddress = custodyWallet.publicKey;
console.log(`Custody wallets configured: ${data.wallets.length}`);
console.log(`Deployment wallet: ${signingCustodyWalletId}`);
```

A working setup prints:

```text title="Output"
Custody wallets configured: 2
Deployment wallet: cwlt_123
```

If the response includes an active wallet with `isRuntimeExecutionAllowed: true`, your custody is
bound. You are ready to deploy a token.

If the response returns no wallets, your custody provider has not finished provisioning. For the
Anchorage pipeline, contact your onboarding lead. For the self-serve sandbox, wait a minute and run
the call again. Privy's first wallet provision can lag the SDP organization creation by a few
seconds.

Keep both values. `signingCustodyWalletId` is the SDP wallet record `id` (`cwlt_*`) that issuance
requests use. It is not the provider-specific `walletId`, and it is not the Solana `publicKey`.
`custodyAddress` is that public key. Use it only where an onchain address is required.

## 3. Design the token

Before any API call, decide three things: which template to start from, what compliance posture the
token deploys with, and which authorities the custodian holds. Your compliance officer reviews this
design. The API calls in Section 4 are the mechanical follow-through.

### Pick the template

A **Tokenization Template** prescribes a fixed set of
[Token-2022](https://solana.com/docs/tokens/extensions) extensions for one class of institutional
product. Call `GET /v1/issuance/templates` to list the templates available to your project and the
defaults each one applies.

Three of those templates matter here:

- **`stablecoin`**. 6 decimals by default. Required extensions: `permanentDelegate` and `pausable`.
  The **Token Access Control** allowlist is off. Use this template for a regulated dollar.
- **`tokenized-security`**. 8 decimals. Required extensions: `permanentDelegate` and `pausable`.
  The `scaledUiAmount` extension is available on this template, but it is opt-in rather than
  required. The Token Access Control allowlist is on, and accounts open frozen. Use this template
  for a regulated security.
- **`custom`**. 9 decimals. No required extensions. Use this template only when neither template
  above fits.

This tutorial uses `stablecoin`. Its required extensions are what a US permitted payment stablecoin
issuer needs to satisfy the technological-capability mandate in the GENIUS Act. Section 5 covers
that mandate.

### Set the compliance posture

Four fields on token creation determine the posture you deploy with. Three of them are booleans.
The fourth, `maxSupply`, is an optional decimal string.

- **`isFreezable`**. Set it to `true`. If it is `false` at create time, the token deploys with no
  freeze authority, and you cannot freeze an account afterward.
- **`isMintable`**. Set it to `true` for an active stablecoin. You mint as new fiat reserves arrive
  at the custody bank.
- **`requiresAllowlist`**. Turns on the allowlist mode of Token Access Control. Only listed
  addresses can then receive the token. Leave it off for a payment stablecoin. The institutional
  pattern is to screen before each transfer, not to gate by allowlist. The `tokenized-security`
  template turns this on automatically.
- **`maxSupply`**. An optional supply cap, written as a decimal string in display units. Use it for
  a pilot program with a hard ceiling. Omit it for uncapped supply.

### Plan the authorities

A regulated stablecoin has five onchain authorities. Each one is a distinct role.

- **`mint`**. Authorizes new supply.
- **`freeze`**. Freezes and unfreezes one token account.
- **`permanentDelegate`**. Moves or burns any holder's tokens without their signature. This is the
  technological capability that the GENIUS Act requires for lawful orders.
- **`metadata`**. Updates the token's onchain metadata.
- **The pause authority**. Pauses and resumes all transfers. It lives on the `pausable` extension
  configuration rather than on the mint.

At deploy, SDP sets the first four authorities to your custody signer. SDP sets the pause authority
to the `mint` authority unless you set it explicitly.

You can delegate or revoke any authority later with
`POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/authority`. Leaving every authority with the custodian is the
institutional baseline.

### Capture the design as a config

Section 4 takes one input: a configuration object that holds the design choices above. This is the
Treasury Pilot USD example that the rest of the tutorial uses.

```javascript title="token-config.js"
const tokenConfig = {
  template: "stablecoin",
  name: "Treasury Pilot USD",
  symbol: "TPUSD",
  decimals: 6,
  signingCustodyWalletId,
  description: "GENIUS-compliant treasury pilot stablecoin.",
  maxSupply: "100000000",
  isFreezable: true,
  isMintable: true,
};
```

Your design is captured. You are ready to make the first state-mutating call.

## 4. Create and deploy the token

Two API calls take the design from an object literal to a deployed stablecoin on Solana. The first
call creates the record. The second call deploys it onchain. Both run from the Developer key
(`sdp`).

### Create the token record

The first call writes the token's metadata to SDP's database. Nothing happens on Solana yet. The
token starts at `status: "pending"` with no `mintAddress`.

```javascript title="create-token.js"
const created = await sdp.post("/v1/issuance/tokens", tokenConfig);
const tokenId = created.data.token.id;
```

A successful response:

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "token": {
      "id": "tok_e152fd38-...",
      "template": "stablecoin",
      "symbol": "TPUSD",
      "decimals": 6,
      "status": "pending",
      "signingCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
      "mintAddress": null,
      "isFreezable": true,
      "isMintable": true,
      "requiresAllowlist": false,
      "maxSupply": "100000000"
    }
  }
}
```

Save the `tok_*` ID. The deploy call uses it.

### Deploy the token onchain

The deploy call submits a Token-2022 mint creation transaction to Solana through the custody
signer. SDP then updates the token record with the resulting onchain addresses.

```javascript title="deploy-token.js"
const deployKey = idempotencyKey("deploy");
const deployed = await sdp.post(
  `/v1/issuance/tokens/${tokenId}/deploy`,
  { signingCustodyWalletId },
  { idempotencyKey: deployKey }
);
const mintAddress = deployed.data.token.mintAddress;
```

A successful response carries the deployed token record. The record has `status: "active"` and a
populated onchain `mintAddress`.

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "token": {
      "id": "tok_e152fd38-...",
      "status": "active",
      "signingCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
      "mintAddress": "6V5bTuMsmXyhdY2Hj6VWQZsuacugACBmPqNtQgGtar8L",
      "mintAuthority": "ASy986dzvVqHHV2Ftfe9ZKshKZhEEQwuAoPoKMc64A9X",
      "freezeAuthority": "ASy986dzvVqHHV2Ftfe9ZKshKZhEEQwuAoPoKMc64A9X",
      "metadataAuthority": "ASy986dzvVqHHV2Ftfe9ZKshKZhEEQwuAoPoKMc64A9X",
      "extensions": {
        "defaultAccountState": "initialized",
        "permanentDelegate": "ASy986dzvVqHHV2Ftfe9ZKshKZhEEQwuAoPoKMc64A9X"
      },
      "deployedAt": "2026-05-18T14:50:43.329Z"
    }
  }
}
```

The `mintAuthority`, `freezeAuthority`, and `metadataAuthority` all resolve to the public key of
the `signingCustodyWalletId` you supplied. SDP sets the `permanentDelegate` at the same time. It
appears on the token record's `extensions.permanentDelegate` field rather than as a top-level
authority.

After deployment, the token's `signingCustodyWalletId` records historical attribution. It is not a
preferred signer, and it is not a fallback. SDP checks an authority-gated operation against the
live onchain authority, and a standard burn uses its own source wallet.

<Callout type="warn">
Deploy can return a bare `500 INTERNAL_ERROR` with no `details` field. The most common cause on
devnet is an unfunded custody wallet. Section 2 covers funding it from the browser faucet. Any
other downstream Solana RPC failure also appears this way.

Fund the custody wallet from the faucet. Then call `/deploy` again with the same `Idempotency-Key`
to replay the prior result, or with a fresh key to make a new attempt. SDP treats different keys as
different requests.
</Callout>

### Confirm the deploy

Confirm that the onchain state matches the record before you move to Section 5.

```javascript title="confirm-deploy.js"
const { data } = await sdp.get(`/v1/issuance/tokens/${tokenId}`);
console.log(`Status: ${data.token.status}`);
console.log(`Mint:   ${data.token.mintAddress}`);
```

A working deploy prints:

```text title="Output"
Status: active
Mint:   6V5bTuMsmXyhdY2Hj6VWQZsuacugACBmPqNtQgGtar8L
```

The same state appears in the SDP dashboard's issuance page.

![Deployed token shown in the SDP dashboard's issuance page, with status active and the mint address displayed.](/issue-a-regulated-stablecoin/02-deployed-token-dashboard.png)

The token is deployed. Section 5 configures the compliance controls that the GENIUS Act requires
before any tokens move.

## 5. Configure compliance controls

This section covers the controls that the regulation requires.

Section 4(a)(5) of the GENIUS Act treats a permitted payment stablecoin issuer as a financial
institution for the purposes of the Bank Secrecy Act. That sentence is what makes everything below
load-bearing.

The Act also requires you to have "[the technological capability to comply with all lawful orders to seize, freeze, burn or prevent the transfer of outstanding stablecoins](https://www.skadden.com/insights/publications/2025/07/us-establishes-first-federal-regulatory-framework)."
The endpoints in this section map onto that phrase, in the order you meet them. Screening comes
first. Freeze blocks one account. Seize recovers tokens. Force-burn is the final remedy.

The issuance selectors below reuse the `signingCustodyWalletId` from Section 2. SDP verifies that
this wallet controls the live freeze or permanent-delegate authority before it signs.

### Screen before you move funds

Screen every transfer destination and every allowlist entry before your application acts on it.
Screening takes one API call.

```javascript title="screen-address.js"
const response = await sdpAdmin.post("/v1/compliance/address-screenings", {
  address: destinationAddress,
  network: "solana",
  intent: "transfer_destination",
});

for (const provider of response.data.screening.providers) {
  if (provider.status === "error" || provider.riskScore > THRESHOLD) {
    throw new TransferBlocked(provider);
  }
}
```

SDP integrates with four screening providers: Range, Elliptic, TRM, and Chainalysis. SDP enables no
compliance provider by default, so an administrator configures the providers for your organization
first.

One call then fans out to every configured provider and returns one array entry per provider. Write
your code against that array rather than against a named provider. Iterate over `providers[]`. Fail
closed on any `status: "error"` and on any threshold breach.

A single provider can be unavailable for credential reasons or rate-limit reasons. A fail-closed
policy keeps you defensible when one feed degrades.

On the sandbox response that this tutorial cites, Range and Elliptic return numeric scores. TRM
returns a healthy status without scoring a fresh address. Chainalysis returns an upstream
credential error. Treat each provider's verdict as one signal. Your policy must not depend on a
single provider's availability.

### Freeze one account

A freeze halts one holder's account and touches no other holder. The freeze is onchain, and the
Token-2022 program enforces it. SDP signs the freeze instruction with the freeze authority that was
set at deploy.

```javascript title="freeze-account.js"
const holderFreezeKey = idempotencyKey("freeze");
await sdpAdmin.post(
  `/v1/issuance/tokens/${tokenId}/freeze`,
  {
    signingCustodyWalletId,
    accountAddress: holderAddress,
    reason: "Court order #2026-IL-0142",
  },
  { idempotencyKey: holderFreezeKey }
);
```

Pass the holder's wallet address. SDP derives the
[Associated Token Account](https://solana.com/docs/tokens/basics/create-token-account) that holds
that holder's TPUSD balance, and freezes it. Once the account is frozen, transfers to it and from
it fail at the program level, not at SDP's gateway.

Section 7 runs this block live and shows the error that the frozen account returns.

### Seize tokens for compliance recovery

A seize moves tokens out of a holder's account without their signature. It uses the **permanent
delegate** authority that was set at deploy.

The permanent delegate is a Token-2022 extension. It grants a named authority the right to transfer
or burn any holder's tokens, whatever the holder signs. This is the technological capability that
the GENIUS Act requires you to have ready for lawful orders. The institutional use case is a
court-ordered transfer, or a sanctions matter where you must recover specific tokens to a
controlled wallet.

```javascript title="seize-tokens.js"
const seizeKey = idempotencyKey("seize");
await sdpAdmin.post(
  `/v1/issuance/tokens/${tokenId}/seize`,
  {
    signingCustodyWalletId,
    seize: {
      source: holderAddress,
      destination: custodyAddress,
      amount: "50000.00",
      memo: "OFAC matter 2026-04-018",
    },
  },
  { idempotencyKey: seizeKey }
);
```

SDP stores the memo on the transaction record. The memo is the audit attribution that your
compliance officer reads months later, when they reconcile the action against the court order or
the sanctions notice that authorized it.

### Force-burn as the final remedy

A force-burn destroys tokens in a holder's account. It uses the same authority as a seize, with a
different effect. Use it only when you cannot recover the tokens to a controlled wallet. One
example is a self-custodied address whose key you cannot obtain.

```javascript title="force-burn.js"
const forceBurnKey = idempotencyKey("force-burn");
await sdpAdmin.post(
  `/v1/issuance/tokens/${tokenId}/force-burn`,
  {
    signingCustodyWalletId,
    forceBurn: {
      source: holderAddress,
      amount: "12000.00",
      memo: "regulator-ordered burn 2026-04-021",
    },
  },
  { idempotencyKey: forceBurnKey }
);
```

### Keep the two keys separate

Every endpoint in this section requires the `tokens:admin` permission. Keep two project-scoped API
keys:

- **Developer key**. Routine create, mint, and burn calls.
- **Admin key**. Screen, freeze, seize, and force-burn.

A compliance officer reviewing this design sees a clean separation. Routine issuance cannot
escalate into a compliance action without a deliberate credential change.

Every call writes an entry through SDP's audit service. That trail is the artifact a regulator asks
for, and it is not optional.

## 6. Mint the first tokens

Minting is how new supply enters circulation. For a regulated stablecoin, every mint corresponds to
a fiat reserve event: dollars arrive at the custody bank, the reserve custodian attests to them,
and SDP records the mint against an issuance ticket.

The mint call is small. What you put in the memo field is what your compliance officer reconciles
against the reserve report.

### Send the mint call

Minting requires the `tokens:write` permission, so the Developer key (`sdp`) is the right
credential.

```javascript title="mint-tokens.js"
const mintKey = idempotencyKey("mint");
const minted = await sdp.post(
  `/v1/issuance/tokens/${tokenId}/mint`,
  {
    signingCustodyWalletId,
    mint: {
      destination: custodyAddress,
      amount: "1000000",
      memo: "Reserve mint Q2-2026, reference: ANB-RESV-2026-04-091",
    },
  },
  { idempotencyKey: mintKey }
);
```

Four field rules matter here:

- **`signingCustodyWalletId`** is the SDP wallet `id` from Section 2. SDP verifies that this wallet
  controls the current mint authority. SDP does not fall back to the historical deployment wallet.
- **`destination`** is a Solana base58 address. For the initial pattern where the issuer holds the
  supply, this is your custody wallet's public key. For later mints to client wallets, it is the
  recipient's wallet.
- **`amount`** is a decimal string in display units, after decimals are applied. Do not pass a
  number, and do not pass a BigInt. `"1000000"` mints one million TPUSD, because the token has 6
  decimals.
- **`memo`** is up to 100 characters. SDP stores it on the transaction record. This is the
  institutional audit attribution. Your compliance officer uses it months later to reconcile the
  mint against the reserve custodian's monthly report.

### Read the response

A successful mint returns the transaction record and the token account that received the tokens.

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "transaction": {
      "id": "ttx_88240bf5-...",
      "type": "mint",
      "status": "confirmed",
      "signature": "51XZb4Tqm1G4LmSPUwnLrxENWmmhW9UE15LhxrwMrS6vKL4avFzKBBBcPNEQuiMEVgxWRgbdjJERo6K4taQEM9XG",
      "params": {
        "destination": "ASy986dzvVqHHV2Ftfe9ZKshKZhEEQwuAoPoKMc64A9X",
        "amount": "1000000",
        "memo": "Reserve mint Q2-2026, reference: ANB-RESV-2026-04-091",
        "tokenAccount": "NLcEWVJ8oiHdbf6xuSLSAfKfJ1Gqcw4ksYHnkCyEy3t"
      }
    },
    "tokenAccount": "NLcEWVJ8oiHdbf6xuSLSAfKfJ1Gqcw4ksYHnkCyEy3t"
  }
}
```

The `tokenAccount` is the Associated Token Account that holds the newly minted tokens. SDP creates
it on the first mint to that destination if it does not already exist. Later mints to the same
destination reuse it.

### Tie the mint to the reserve attestation

<Callout type="info">
The GENIUS Act requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to publish a monthly public
attestation of reserve composition. A registered public accounting firm signs that attestation, and
the CEO and CFO certify it separately. The mint memo closes the loop on the engineering side of
that obligation.
</Callout>

Every mint memo carries at minimum a reserve reference number. That number maps to one reserve
event in the custodian's records. Two patterns meet the minimum:

- **Single-deposit mint**: `"ANB-RESV-2026-04-091"`. This is the deposit reference that the custody
  bank assigned when it received the fiat reserves.
- **Batched mint against a reserve commitment**: `"Q2-2026 commitment tranche 3 of 6"`. This is a
  pre-arranged reserve commitment, broken into scheduled releases.

Do not write a mint memo that cannot be matched to a reserve record. The compliance officer reading
the attestation report needs a one-to-one mapping, and the auditor signing the report depends on
it.

### Confirm the supply

```javascript title="confirm-supply.js"
const { data } = await sdp.get(`/v1/issuance/tokens/${tokenId}`);
console.log(`Total supply: ${data.token.totalSupply}`);
```

Prints:

```text title="Output"
Total supply: 1000000
```

Tokens are in circulation. Section 7 tests the compliance controls from Section 5 against a live
transfer.

## 7. Test a transfer and a compliance action

The compliance controls in Section 5 matter only if they enforce. This section moves tokens between
two wallets, then tests the freeze authority live.

### Send a clean transfer

Transfers run on the `/v1/payments/transfers` endpoints, which are separate from the issuance
endpoints that Section 4 used. The call requires the `payments:write` and `wallets:read`
permissions. The Developer key (`sdp`) carries both.

```javascript title="transfer-tokens.js"
const sourceCustodyWalletId = signingCustodyWalletId;

const screening = await sdpAdmin.post("/v1/compliance/address-screenings", {
  address: destinationAddress,
  network: "solana",
  intent: "transfer_destination",
});

for (const provider of screening.data.screening.providers) {
  if (provider.status === "error" || provider.riskScore > THRESHOLD) {
    throw new TransferBlocked(provider);
  }
}

const transfer = await sdp.post(
  "/v1/payments/transfers",
  {
    sourceCustodyWalletId,
    destination: destinationAddress,
    token: mintAddress,
    amount: "100",
    memo: "Treasury Pilot internal transfer #042",
  },
  { idempotencyKey: idempotencyKey("transfer") }
);
```

Three field rules matter here:

- **`sourceCustodyWalletId`** is the SDP wallet `id` (`cwlt_*`) that `GET /v1/wallets` returns. It
  is not the wallet's public key, and it is not the provider-specific `walletId`.
- **`token`** is the onchain mint address from the deploy response in Section 4. It is not the SDP
  token ID (`tok_*`).
- **`destination`** is any valid Solana base58 address. It does not have to be a wallet that SDP
  knows about.

A successful response includes the onchain signature once the transaction confirms.

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "transfer": {
      "id": "xfr_f570debc-...",
      "type": "transfer",
      "direction": "outbound",
      "status": "confirmed",
      "custodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
      "providerWalletId": "privy_jfxdbsq4bg6dxzsd7imgon3j",
      "signature": "ekNe4HK67AXptsx6krYATZd5xYeq8wYQShmN9oHUdAipVJVFELGwiLhdJNCAbyN2TPv9SwzBTNz6igoAfWTdCYP",
      "source": "ASy986dzvVqHHV2Ftfe9ZKshKZhEEQwuAoPoKMc64A9X",
      "destination": "2H2w3hSxAPTybuTL7LkhPbyk6bWYi94x2J4aqBhhyJL2",
      "token": "6V5bTuMsmXyhdY2Hj6VWQZsuacugACBmPqNtQgGtar8L",
      "amount": "100",
      "memo": "Treasury Pilot internal transfer #042"
    }
  }
}
```

### Freeze the destination

Freeze the destination's TPUSD account with the Admin key. Freeze requires `tokens:admin`, which
the Developer key does not carry.

```javascript title="freeze-destination.js"
const transferFreezeKey = idempotencyKey("freeze");
await sdpAdmin.post(
  `/v1/issuance/tokens/${tokenId}/freeze`,
  {
    signingCustodyWalletId,
    accountAddress: destinationAddress,
    reason: "Compliance hold pending OFAC review 2026-04-019",
  },
  { idempotencyKey: transferFreezeKey }
);
```

The freeze records a frozen account in SDP's audit trail. It also applies the Token-2022 freeze
instruction to the destination's Associated Token Account onchain. You can verify the onchain side
on Solana Explorer.

![Freeze transaction on Solana Explorer in devnet, showing the Token-2022 FreezeAccount instruction applied to the destination's associated token account.](/issue-a-regulated-stablecoin/03-freeze-on-chain-explorer.png)

### Attempt the transfer again

Run the same transfer call. This time it fails.

```javascript title="transfer-blocked.js"
try {
  await sdp.post(
    "/v1/payments/transfers",
    {
      sourceCustodyWalletId,
      destination: destinationAddress,
      token: mintAddress,
      amount: "100",
      memo: "Compliance test, expecting block",
    },
    { idempotencyKey: idempotencyKey("blocked-transfer") }
  );
} catch (error) {
  // handle the onchain block (see the error-handling section below)
}
```

SDP returns this error envelope, with HTTP status 502:

```json title="response.json"
{
  "error": {
    "code": "SOLANA_RPC_ERROR",
    "message": "Failed to sign and send transaction: RPC Error -32000: Invalid transaction: Transaction simulation failed: Error processing Instruction 1: custom program error: 0x11"
  }
}
```

This is the one error pattern to learn from this tutorial, and it is the reason the envelope reads
the way it does.

The outer code, `SOLANA_RPC_ERROR`, names the family of failure. It tells you that an upstream call
failed. It is not the compliance verdict. The reason lives in the wrapped message:
`custom program error: 0x11`. That is Token-2022's `AccountFrozen` signal, decimal 17. The
Token-2022 program enforced the block onchain. SDP's gateway did not.

Treat `0x11` as a compliance verdict, not as a failure you can retry. The same rule applies
whenever SDP wraps a downstream Solana RPC error: the outer code is the family of failure, and the
wrapped code is the actual reason.

### Parse the wrapped error

Write your error handler against the wrapped onchain code rather than against the outer SDP code.

```javascript title="parse-error.js"
function isOnChainCompliance(error) {
  return error.message?.includes("custom program error: 0x11");
}

try {
  // transfer attempt
} catch (error) {
  if (isOnChainCompliance(error)) {
    // log to the compliance system, do not retry
    return reportToCompliance(error);
  }
  // anything else: treat as a transient RPC failure and apply your retry policy
  throw error;
}
```

### Clean up

In production, you unfreeze only after the underlying compliance review resolves. In the sandbox,
you can unfreeze immediately.

```javascript title="unfreeze-account.js"
await sdpAdmin.post(`/v1/issuance/tokens/${tokenId}/unfreeze`, {
  signingCustodyWalletId,
  accountAddress: destinationAddress,
});
```

The freeze is cleared, so the destination can receive transfers again. Section 8 covers the
production transition. It lists what changes between `sk_test_` and `sk_live_`, and which checks
your compliance officer signs against before this same code runs on mainnet.

## 8. Production transition checklist

The work between `sk_test_` and `sk_live_` is not a flag change. It is the moment your compliance
officer signs against the runbook your engineering team has built since Section 2.

Going to production changes six artifacts mechanically. It also adds a longer list of items that
your institution attests to.

### What changes mechanically

Your sandbox setup rests on six artifacts. Each one swaps for a production equivalent.

- **API keys**. Replace your project-scoped Developer and Admin keys with `sk_live_` keys minted
  from your production project. Use the bootstrap pattern from Section 2 with a fresh Admin key.
  Select the `default-production` project from `GET /v1/projects` instead of `default-sandbox`, and
  mint fresh project-scoped keys under it.
- **Custody provider**. In production, `provider` names your federally chartered custodian. For
  most US institutional issuers that is Anchorage Digital Bank, bound to your organization through
  the Anchorage onboarding flow. The Privy sandbox wallets do not carry over.
- **Solana cluster**. Mainnet replaces devnet. Your custody bank funds the custody address as part
  of its standard operational support. You do not use a faucet.
- **API base URL**. `https://api.solana.com` is the base URL in production and in sandbox. It does
  not change.
- **Screening providers**. Confirm that the production provider mix matches your compliance team's
  policy. Run `POST /v1/compliance/address-screenings` against a known address before live traffic.
  Confirm that every provider your policy depends on returns `status: "ok"`, and that your handler
  fails closed for any provider that does not.
- **Idempotency-Key strategy**. In production, generate idempotency keys deterministically per
  operation, for example `mint-${reserveDepositReference}`. Do not generate a random key per
  attempt. A deterministic key lets your runbook resend a call safely without minting twice.

### What your compliance officer signs off on

Before any `sk_live_` key sees real traffic, your compliance officer needs evidence that the
posture from Section 1 is operational rather than aspirational. This is the minimum sign-off list.

- **GENIUS Section 4(a)(5) capabilities demonstrated**. Screening, freeze, seize, and force-burn
  each exercised in the sandbox, with a captured response in the audit trail.
- **BSA/AML program documented**. A written risk-based policy with internal controls, ongoing
  customer due diligence, and independent testing. A US-located AML/CFT compliance officer named,
  under proposed 31 CFR § 1033.210 in the FinCEN and OFAC implementing rules.
- **Sanctions program ready**. An OFAC screening provider configured and tested, the technical
  capability to block transactions in place, and a defined secondary-market screening procedure.
- **Reserve attestation cadence agreed**. A registered public accounting firm engaged, a monthly
  examination schedule signed, and a defined CEO and CFO certification process.
- **Audit trail review**. SDP's audit-service entries reviewed for completeness. The mint memos
  from Section 6 reconcile to reserve references in the custody bank's records.
- **Incident response runbook**. The operational playbook for a freeze, seize, or force-burn order.
  It states what happens when a court order arrives, who signs in with which credential, how long
  the chain of custody runs, and where the documentation lands.

### The cutover

When the sign-off is in, the cutover itself is small.

1. Repeat the bootstrap from Section 2 with `environment: "production"`.
2. Mint your production keys.
3. Store the keys with your other live secrets.
4. Update your runtime environment.
5. Run the wallet verification call from Section 2 against the production API base, to confirm that
   the wallets are bound.

Your first production mint corresponds to a real fiat reserve event at your custody bank.

## 9. What to read next

You have a deployed regulated stablecoin, the compliance controls configured, and a production
transition checklist that your compliance officer can sign against. That is the issuance side of
the institutional product.

Two adjacent problems build on it, and SDP does not yet publish a tutorial for either one.

**Tokenizing a treasury fund.** A tokenized money market fund or treasury bond product uses the
`tokenized-security` template. Its compliance posture differs from the stablecoin pattern in three
ways: the allowlist is on by default, accounts open frozen, and the `scaledUiAmount` extension is
available for accrued yield. Most of the Section 5 controls work identically. The differences sit
in the design and deploy steps in Sections 3 and 4. See
[Token templates](/docs/reference/issuance-token-types) for the template defaults, and
[Tokenize an asset](/docs/tokens/tokenize-an-asset) for the decision between token models.

**Running enterprise stablecoin payments.** Institutional payment flows pick up after Section 7.
They cover bulk transfers, scheduled payments, onramp and offramp integration with custody bank
settlement, and the policy-engine patterns that gate transfers at scale. See
[Payments](/docs/payments) for the transfer endpoints and
[Wallet policies](/docs/wallet-operations/policies) for the policy engine.

### Reference docs

For API details beyond this tutorial:

- [SDP API reference](/docs/reference/api). The generated endpoint inventory across all public API
  families.
- [SDP Postman collection](/docs/reference/postman-collection). An importable request bundle for
  the full API.
- [Token-2022 program documentation](https://solana.com/docs/tokens/extensions). The onchain
  program that SDP wraps.
- [GENIUS Act analysis](https://www.gibsondunn.com/the-genius-act-a-new-era-of-stablecoin-regulation/).
  Statutory interpretation covering each subsection of the Act.
- [FinCEN and OFAC implementing rules NPRM](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/10/2026-06963/permitted-payment-stablecoin-issuer-anti-money-launderingcountering-the-financing-of-terrorism).
  The current implementing-rule source for the BSA designation in GENIUS Section 4(a)(5).

---

### End-to-end payment flow
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/tutorials/end-to-end-payment-flow

> The stages of an SDP payment, from the funding wallet to reconciliation in your ledger.

This page lists the stages of a payment integration in order. It does not contain code or endpoint
details. Use it as a checklist, then follow the API reference links below for each call.

1. Create the funding wallet, or look up an existing one.
2. Choose the amount, the destination address, and the token for the transfer.
3. Validate those three values against your own rules.
4. Submit the transfer.
5. Store the identifiers that the response returns.
6. Poll the transfer status until the transfer is finalized.
7. Reconcile the finalized transfer with your product ledger.
8. Update the state that your users see.

When you submit the transfer, SDP builds the transaction, signs it with the source custody wallet,
and submits it to the Solana cluster.

Use the [Payments API reference](/docs/reference/api/payments) and [Wallets API reference](/docs/reference/api/wallets) for endpoint-level request and response details.

---

## Self-Hosting

### Overview
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting

> Run the Solana Developer Platform on your own infrastructure with Docker Compose.

Self-hosting runs the full Solana Developer Platform on infrastructure you control, from prebuilt
container images. The stack includes the API, the dashboard, the documentation site, a database,
and a cache. You bring your own authentication provider, Solana RPC endpoint, and signing provider.
SDP is the same product you would use as a managed service.

This section covers installing the stack, generating its configuration, and keeping it running.

## Requirements

- A 64-bit Linux or macOS host with **Docker Engine** and **Docker Compose v2**.
- Outbound network access to pull the images and to reach your Solana RPC endpoint and your
  authentication provider.
- A [Clerk](https://clerk.com) application for authentication, and a Solana RPC endpoint. See the
  [environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference) for the full list.

Use a dedicated endpoint from an RPC provider. The public devnet endpoint
`https://api.devnet.solana.com` rejects `getTokenAccountsByOwner`, so wallet balances do not load
against it.

## Services in the stack

One `compose.yml` file defines the stack. It lives at `infra/self-hosted/compose.yml` in the SDP
repository, and the install script downloads the released copy of that same file into `~/sdp` on
your host.

`compose.yml` starts six services. It pulls each SDP image from the registry in
`SDP_IMAGE_REGISTRY`, at the tag in `SDP_VERSION`. The table shows the default registry, and `<tag>`
stands for the tag you run.

| Service | Image | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `sdp-api` | `ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp/sdp-api:<tag>` | The core API (default port `8787`). |
| `sdp-web` | `ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp/sdp-web:<tag>` | The dashboard web app (default port `3000`). |
| `sdp-docs` | `ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp/sdp-docs:<tag>` | The Solana Developer Platform documentation site (default port `3001`). |
| `sdp-migrate` | `ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp/sdp-api:<tag>` | Runs database migrations once on startup, then exits. |
| `postgres` | `postgres:16-alpine` | Bundled database (or point at an external one). |
| `redis` | `redis:7-alpine` | Bundled cache (or point at an external one). |

## Installation and configuration

- **[Quickstart](/docs/self-hosting/quickstart)** installs the stack and brings it up for the first
  time.
- **[First devnet deployment](/docs/self-hosting/first-devnet-deployment)** shows you how to log
  into the dashboard, initialize a local wallet, and verify a wallet-scoped API key.
- **[Configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator)** generates a complete `.env` file in your
  browser or your terminal.
- **[Environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference)** explains what every configuration
  variable does and which ones are required.

## Operation and maintenance

- **[Upgrade and backup](/docs/self-hosting/upgrade-and-backup)** moves the stack to a new release
  and protects your data.
- **[Troubleshooting](/docs/self-hosting/troubleshooting)** lists the common startup and
  configuration failures and how to fix them.
- **[External co-signers](/docs/self-hosting/external-co-signers)** explains how to host
  provider-specific signing automation alongside the stack.

---

### Quickstart
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/quickstart

> Install the self-hosted stack, generate a .env file, and bring it up with Docker Compose.

This guide takes you from an empty host to a running Solana Developer Platform. It assumes that
**Docker Engine** and **Docker Compose v2** are installed, and that the Docker daemon is running.

## 1. Install

The install script downloads `compose.yml` and `.env.example` for the latest release into `~/sdp`.
It then verifies both files against the release checksums.

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -fsSL https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
```

The script is open source. You can read it before you run it, and you can verify the checksums and
the signature out of band. The commented header of `install.sh` documents the full verified-install
flow. It also documents the environment variables you can override, such as `SDP_INSTALL_DIR` and
`INSTALL_VERSION`.

You can also install by hand. Download `compose.yml` and `.env.example` from the
[latest release](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/releases/latest)
into a working directory of your choice.

## 2. Generate your `.env`

The stack reads its configuration from a `.env` file next to `compose.yml`. The
[configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator) fills that file in for you. It generates the app
secrets and validates your answers.

- **In your browser.** Open the [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator), answer the
  prompts, and download the `.env` file into `~/sdp`.
- **In your terminal.** Run the configurator from the API image:

  ```bash title="Terminal"
  docker run --rm -it -v "$HOME/sdp:/out" \
    ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp/sdp-api:latest \
    node configure.js --out /out/.env
  ```

  Replace `latest` with the release tag you installed, so that the configurator matches your
  `compose.yml`.

See the [environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference) for what each variable means and
which ones are required.

## 3. Bring up the stack

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose up -d
```

On startup, `sdp-migrate` runs the database migrations once. The API, web, and docs services start
after it finishes. The first run pulls the images, so it can take a few minutes.

## 4. Verify

```bash title="Terminal"
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f sdp-api
```

When the services report healthy, the dashboard is at `http://localhost:3000` and the API is at
`http://localhost:8787`. The self-hosted documentation site is at `http://localhost:3001`.

The API has a [health endpoint](/docs/reference/api/health). You can poll it from a load balancer
or from an uptime check.

If a service fails to start, or a required variable is missing, see
[Troubleshooting](/docs/self-hosting/troubleshooting).

## Next steps

- [First devnet deployment](/docs/self-hosting/first-devnet-deployment) shows you how to log into
  the dashboard, initialize a local wallet, and verify API access.
- [Upgrade and backup](/docs/self-hosting/upgrade-and-backup) keeps the stack current and protects
  your data.
- [Environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference) explains how to change ports, RPC,
  signing, and authentication.

---

### First devnet deployment
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/first-devnet-deployment

> Run self-hosted SDP on devnet, log into the dashboard, initialize a local wallet, and verify API access.

This tutorial takes a fresh self-hosted install from healthy containers to the first useful devnet
workflow. You log into the dashboard, initialize a local wallet, create a wallet-scoped API key, and
make an authenticated API call.

Use this page after the [Quickstart](/docs/self-hosting/quickstart). The path here runs on devnet
only, and it uses the default local signer. Set up a provider-specific signer in a later hardening
pass.

<Callout type="warn">
The public Solana devnet RPC endpoint is useful for a smoke test. It can also be rate-limited or
incomplete for balance-heavy wallet pages. The public endpoint `https://api.devnet.solana.com`
rejects `getTokenAccountsByOwner`, so wallet balances do not load against it. Use a dedicated devnet
endpoint from an RPC provider before you treat this flow as reliable.
</Callout>

<Steps>

<Step>

## Confirm the stack is healthy

Run these commands from the directory where the installer placed `compose.yml` and `.env`:

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
curl http://localhost:8787/health
```

The health call returns a JSON response with `status: "ok"`. The dashboard is at
`http://localhost:3000` and the API is at `http://localhost:8787`. The self-hosted documentation
site is at `http://localhost:3001`.

</Step>

<Step>

## Configure Clerk for dashboard login

Work in your Clerk development app:

- Copy the publishable key, the secret key, and the issuer into the
  [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator).
- Customize the session token in the Clerk dashboard, under **Sessions** and then **Customize
  session token**. Use the claims from the
  [Clerk setup guide](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/blob/main/apps/sdp-api/docs/self-hosting/clerk-setup.md).
- Expose your local API with the webhook tunnel. Reserve a free stable domain at
  [dashboard.ngrok.com/domains](https://dashboard.ngrok.com/domains), set it as
  `WEBHOOK_INGEST_DOMAIN` in `apps/sdp-api/.env.local`, and run `pnpm dev:webhooks`.
- Create a webhook endpoint that points at `https://<your-domain>/webhooks/clerk/link-orgs`. Clerk
  delivers over the public internet, so it cannot reach `localhost` directly.
- Copy the webhook signing secret into `CLERK_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.

Raw environment validation treats `CLERK_WEBHOOK_SECRET` as optional. This tutorial requires it,
because the webhook is what creates the local SDP organization record after dashboard signup.

</Step>

<Step>

## Generate the devnet `.env`

Open the [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator) and keep the defaults for the first
deployment. Fill in the following:

- `SOLANA_RPC_URL` with a devnet RPC endpoint.
- The Clerk publishable key, secret key, issuer, and webhook secret.
- Local signing with native fee payment.

The signing step generates a local Solana signer in the browser. It then shows the public key that
you fund on devnet. Save the generated file as `~/sdp/.env`, then restart the stack:

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose up -d
```

<Callout type="info">
In self-hosted mode, SDP entitles every provider that is configured in the environment. A provider
that is not configured stays unavailable. The default devnet path therefore offers only the local
signer.
</Callout>

</Step>

<Step>

## Log into the dashboard

Open `http://localhost:3000` and sign in through Clerk. Create or join an organization when the
dashboard prompts you. After the Clerk webhook lands, the dashboard shows the organization and
project context instead of onboarding errors.

If the dashboard loads but the organization state does not appear, check the API logs:

```bash title="Terminal"
docker compose logs -f sdp-api
```

Look for Clerk webhook errors, session token claim mismatches, or a missing
`CLERK_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.

</Step>

<Step>

## Initialize a local custody wallet

In the dashboard, open **Wallets**. Choose the local provider. Create a wallet named
`Devnet local wallet`.

You can also use the API path. Use an admin key from the dashboard:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST http://localhost:8787/v1/wallets/initialize \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "provider": "local",
    "walletLabel": "Devnet local wallet"
  }'
```

Copy the returned `walletId`. You bind the API key to this wallet in the next step.

</Step>

<Step>

## Create a wallet-scoped API key

Open **API keys** in the dashboard and create a **Sandbox** key. A Sandbox key targets the devnet
cluster, which is what this tutorial uses.

Choose **Selected wallets**. Select the local wallet you created in the previous step. Set it as
the key's default wallet.

Save the full key while the dashboard shows it. SDP displays it only once.

</Step>

<Step>

## Verify the key can read wallets

Use the new key against your self-hosted API:

```bash title="Terminal"
export SDP_API_KEY="sk_test_..."

curl "http://localhost:8787/v1/wallets?view=summary" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SDP_API_KEY"
```

The response includes the local wallet you created. You now have a self-hosted devnet stack with
dashboard authentication, local custody signing, and an API key bound to the one wallet it is
allowed to use.

</Step>

</Steps>

## Next steps

- Use the [Environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference) to move from localhost defaults
  to real domains, an external Postgres, or an external Redis.
- Use [Upgrade and backup](/docs/self-hosting/upgrade-and-backup) before you keep meaningful
  operator data in the stack.
- Use [External co-signers](/docs/self-hosting/external-co-signers) when a provider requires an
  extra signing process outside the default compose stack.

### Configurator
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/configurator

> Generate a complete .env file for a self-hosted Solana Developer Platform, entirely in your browser.

Use the guided steps below to generate a `.env` file for the default devnet self-hosting path.
Everything runs in your browser. Nothing you enter is sent anywhere.

Put the downloaded file next to `compose.yml`, then run `docker compose up -d`.

For the full operator walkthrough after the download, continue with
[First devnet deployment](/docs/self-hosting/first-devnet-deployment).

<EnvConfigurator />

---

### Environment reference
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/env-reference

> The configuration variables a self-hosted Solana Developer Platform reads from .env.

The self-hosted stack reads its configuration from a single `.env` file next to `compose.yml`.

The [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator) is the authoritative source of the field list,
the defaults, and the validation. It always matches the release you installed. This page explains
how the configuration is organized, and it covers the variables you are most likely to set by hand.

The configurator groups variables into sections:

| Section | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Basic | Core runtime: environment, deployment mode, Transactional Email sender, and Resend key. |
| Database | Bundled Postgres or an external database. |
| Cache | Bundled Redis or an external cache. |
| Solana RPC | Solana cluster and RPC endpoint. |
| Authentication (Clerk) | Required Clerk keys and JWT settings. |
| Signing provider | The signers to enable, and their credentials. |
| Fee payment | How transaction fees are paid. |
| Secrets | App secrets, generated locally. |
| Advanced | Image source, ports, and internal service URLs. |

## Required variables

Set every variable below. The stack refuses to start without them.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` | Password for the bundled Postgres. Always required, because the bundled `postgres` service starts even when the API points at an external `DATABASE_URL`. |
| `API_KEY_PEPPER` | Server-side pepper for API key hashing. Generate it with `openssl rand -hex 32`. |
| `CUSTODY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Encryption key for custody material at rest. Generate it with `openssl rand -base64 32`. |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` | Clerk publishable key for the web app. |
| `CLERK_SECRET_KEY` | Clerk secret key for the API. |
| `CLERK_ISSUER` | Clerk issuer URL used to validate tokens. |
| `SOLANA_RPC_URL` | Solana RPC endpoint the API calls. |
| `SIGNING_PROVIDER` | The default signing provider. Each non-local provider adds its own required credentials. |

The configurator generates `API_KEY_PEPPER` and `CUSTODY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` for you. It can also
generate `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`.

## Database

In the configurator, `DATABASE_MODE` chooses between the bundled Postgres and an external database.
It is a generation-time selector, and the configurator does not write it to `.env`.

For the bundled database, set `POSTGRES_DB`, `POSTGRES_USER`, and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`. The API and
the migration service build their connection string from those three values.

To use an external database, set `DATABASE_URL` to your own `postgresql://…` string. The API and
the migrations then connect there instead. Note that `compose.yml` always starts the bundled
`postgres` container. With an external `DATABASE_URL` that container goes unused, and
`POSTGRES_PASSWORD` is still required for it to start.

The configurator hides `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` once you select an external database. It still writes an
auto-generated value, because the bundled `postgres` container needs one to start even when nothing
connects to it.

## Cache

`CACHE_MODE` works like `DATABASE_MODE`. It is a configurator-only selector, and the configurator
does not write it to `.env`.

To use an external cache, set `REDIS_URL` to your own `redis://…` endpoint. The bundled `redis`
container still starts, and it goes unused.

## Signing providers

`SIGNING_PROVIDER` is the default signer that the configurator writes to `.env`. The supported
values are `local`, `fireblocks`, `privy`, `coinbase_cdp`, `para`, `turnkey`, and `utila`.

The configurator also tracks a `SIGNING_PROVIDERS` selection, which decides the fields it shows.
That key is configurator-only, and the configurator does not write it to `.env`.

Each non-local provider requires its own credentials. Fireblocks, for example, needs an API key, a
secret, and a vault ID. The configurator prompts only for the providers you enable.

Some providers run a co-signer runtime outside the default stack. See
[External co-signers](/docs/self-hosting/external-co-signers).

## Advanced

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `SDP_IMAGE_REGISTRY` | `ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp` | Registry the service images are pulled from. |
| `SDP_VERSION` | `latest` | Image tag for every SDP service. Pin this to a release tag in production. |
| `SDP_API_PORT` | `8787` | Host port for the API. |
| `SDP_WEB_PORT` | `3000` | Host port for the dashboard. |
| `SDP_DOCS_PORT` | `3001` | Host port for the self-hosted documentation site. |
| `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS` | `false` | Trust the first `X-Forwarded-For` address outside Cloud Run. Enable it only behind an ingress that replaces caller-supplied forwarding headers. A direct deployment shares the fail-closed unidentified quota bucket. |

`SDP_API_BASE_URL` defaults to the in-network service name `http://sdp-api:8787`, which
server-to-server calls use.

The browser-facing `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` URLs default to `localhost`, for example `http://localhost:8787`
and `http://localhost:3000`. Change them when you put the services behind your own domains or
ingress.

---

### Upgrade and backup
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/upgrade-and-backup

> Move a self-hosted Solana Developer Platform to a new release and protect its data.

This page covers two operations. It shows how to upgrade to a new release, and how to back up the
data that matters on a self-hosted stack.

## Upgrade to a new release

A release ships new container images and an updated `compose.yml`. Follow these steps:

1. **Refresh the install files.** Run the install script again. It replaces `compose.yml` with the
   new release's version, verified against the release checksums. It leaves any existing `.env` and
   `.env.example` in place. It prints a link to the new release's `.env.example`, so that you can
   check for new variables.

   ```bash title="Terminal"
   curl -fsSL https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
   ```

2. **Pin the version.** Set `SDP_VERSION` in `.env` to the release tag you are upgrading to, rather
   than `latest`. Every service then runs the same, known build.

3. **Pull and restart.**

   ```bash title="Terminal"
   cd ~/sdp
   docker compose pull
   docker compose up -d
   ```

   `sdp-migrate` runs any new database migrations once, before the API starts.

4. **Verify** that the services are healthy, as in the
   [Quickstart](/docs/self-hosting/quickstart#4-verify).

To upgrade to a specific release instead of the latest one, set `INSTALL_VERSION` when you run the
script. Set the matching `SDP_VERSION` in `.env`.

### Roll back a release

Set `SDP_VERSION` back to the previous tag, then run `docker compose up -d`.

Note that SDP does not reverse a migration automatically. If a release applied a migration, restore
from a backup taken before the upgrade. Do not rely on a version downgrade alone.

## Back up your data

Two things hold your state:

- **The Postgres database** holds all platform data. With the bundled database, that data lives in
  the `sdp-postgres-data` Docker volume. With an external `DATABASE_URL`, back the data up with
  your database provider's tooling instead.
- **Your `.env` file** holds the secrets and the configuration. Store it somewhere safe, such as a
  secret manager. You cannot regenerate it identically.

Redis is a cache. You do not need to back it up.

### Back up the database

Take a logical dump with `pg_dump` from the running container. Running it through `sh -c` lets
`pg_dump` read `POSTGRES_USER` and `POSTGRES_DB` from inside the container, so custom values are
honored:

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose exec -T postgres \
  sh -c 'pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" "$POSTGRES_DB"' > sdp-backup.sql
```

Keep these dumps off-host. Take them on a schedule that matches your recovery needs.

### Restore the database

A plain `pg_dump` includes the full schema and the migration history. Restore it into an **empty**
database, and let the stack start on top of it.

Do not restore over a database that is already migrated. The dump's schema then collides with the
schema that `sdp-migrate` created on the previous `up`.

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose down                       # stop every service
docker volume rm sdp_sdp-postgres-data    # discard the current database (destructive)
docker compose up -d postgres             # start a fresh, empty Postgres
until docker compose exec -T postgres \
  sh -c 'pg_isready -U "$POSTGRES_USER"' >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done
docker compose exec -T postgres \
  sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"' < sdp-backup.sql
docker compose up -d                      # start the rest
```

On that final `up`, `sdp-migrate` skips every migration already recorded in the restored dump. A
dump taken at the same release leaves it with nothing to do. An older dump, restored before an
upgrade, lets it apply only the newer migrations.

Restore the matching `.env` file alongside the data, so that secrets such as
`CUSTODY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` line up with the data they protect. For an external `DATABASE_URL`,
restore through your database provider rather than through the bundled `postgres` service.

---

### Troubleshooting
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/troubleshooting

> Diagnose common startup and configuration failures on a self-hosted stack.

Most self-hosting problems appear at startup. Start by looking at the service state and the logs:

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f sdp-api
```

## Docker is not ready

The install script checks for Docker before it does anything else. It reports when Docker is not
installed, when Compose v2 is unavailable, or when the daemon is unreachable. Install or start
Docker, then run the script again. See the
[Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) and
[Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/install/) documentation.

## A required variable is missing

`compose.yml` fails fast when a required variable is unset. The message names the variable, for
example `set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env`.

Confirm that a `.env` file exists next to `compose.yml`, and that it fills in every required
variable. The [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator) produces a complete file. The
[environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference) lists what is required.

## Images do not pull

If `docker compose pull` reports access denied or a missing manifest:

- Confirm that `SDP_IMAGE_REGISTRY` and `SDP_VERSION` point at a registry and a tag you can reach.
- Pull a single image directly to see the underlying error, for example
  `docker pull ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp/sdp-api:latest`.
- Run `docker login` for the registry first, if the registry is private.

## Port already in use

The API, web, and docs services default to ports `8787`, `3000`, and `3001`. A service cannot bind
its port when another process already holds it.

Override the host port in `.env` with `SDP_API_PORT`, `SDP_WEB_PORT`, or `SDP_DOCS_PORT`. Then run
`docker compose up -d` again.

## Migrations failed

`sdp-migrate` runs once before the API starts. The API stays down when it fails. Inspect the
migration logs:

```bash title="Terminal"
docker compose logs sdp-migrate
```

A failure here is usually a database connection problem. Check the `POSTGRES_*` variables, or
`DATABASE_URL`, and confirm that `docker compose ps` reports the `postgres` service as healthy.

## Database connection refused

The API and the migration service wait for Postgres to report healthy before they start. If they
still cannot connect, verify the credentials in `.env`. For an external database, where
`DATABASE_URL` is set, also verify that the database is reachable from inside the Docker network.

## Authentication errors in the dashboard

A sign-in problem points at the Clerk configuration. Re-check
`NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`, `CLERK_SECRET_KEY`, and `CLERK_ISSUER` against your Clerk
application. Confirm that all three keys come from the same Clerk instance, because Clerk issues
separate keys for its development instance and its production instance.

Two sets of environment names meet on this page, and they are not the same thing. Clerk names its
own instances *development* and *production*. SDP names its environments *sandbox* and
*production*, where `sandbox` runs against the Solana devnet cluster and `production` runs against
mainnet. Choose the Clerk instance that matches the deployment you run, and choose the Solana
cluster separately in `SOLANA_RPC_URL`.

## None of these steps fixed the problem

Capture the logs of the failing service, and capture your `.env` settings with the secrets removed.
Then open an issue on the
[project repository](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform).

---

### External co-signers
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/external-co-signers

> Host provider-specific signing automation outside the default self-hosted SDP stack.

Some signing providers need an operator-managed co-signer or automation process in addition to the
SDP API. Run those processes outside the default self-hosted SDP stack.

The self-hosted `compose.yml` stays unchanged by default. It starts the SDP API, the web app, the
docs app, the database, the cache, and the migrations. Provider co-signers are separate operational
services, because they usually have their own secret handling, identity, ingress, and availability
requirements.

## Production pattern

Use a managed container service for a provider-specific co-signer runtime. Google Cloud Run is one
example, and the equivalent service in your own cloud works the same way.

- Use the co-signer image and runtime that the provider or your operator team supplies.
- Store co-signer secrets in a cloud secret manager, not in the SDP compose file.
- Run the co-signer with a dedicated service account. Give that account read access to only the
  secrets it needs.
- Configure ingress and invoker IAM for the provider flow. Prefer private or authenticated ingress
  when the provider does not require a public callback.
- Set `minScale` to `1` when callback latency or provider availability matters. Use scale-to-zero
  only when a cold start is acceptable.
- Keep the development, staging, and production co-signers separated. Separate them by provider
  account, cloud project, service account, and secrets.
- Alert on failed signing attempts, container restarts, authentication failures, and stale or
  expired key material.

## Utila readiness

Utila is the provider that motivates this pattern. When Utila signer support lands, host the
co-signer as an external operator service, for example on Cloud Run. SDP keeps its API, web, docs,
database, and cache inside the normal self-hosted stack.

This page does not make Utila a live SDP signing provider. Do not set `SIGNING_PROVIDER=utila`
until the Utila signer integration adds that provider option and the required runtime
configuration.

Operator scaffolding for a Utila Cloud Run deployment lives in `infra/utila/cloud-run/`. That
scaffold hosts the co-signer endpoint before Utila becomes a default self-hosted service. You can
deploy your own co-signer image, protect the endpoint with Cloud Run IAM or runtime-level request
verification, and pass the resulting service URL and token into a custom SDP Utila integration.
